sections.title: Continuity: the three-condition test

board_events.text: When is a function CONTINUOUS at a point?
Intuition: draw the graph through the point without lifting your pen — no jumps, no holes.
Condition 1: $f(c)$ exists — the function has a definite value at the point.
Condition 2: $\lim_{x\to c} f(x)$ exists — left and right approaches agree.
Condition 3: the limit equals the value — where it heads is where it lands.
All three must hold and agree. Break any one and $f$ is discontinuous.

segments.text: <curious>So when do we call a function continuous at a point? Let's build the idea from the ground up, then make it exam-precise.
Picture riding a train where the rails are joined end to end with no gap. The journey glides through. That unbroken path is continuity — you draw the graph through the point without lifting your pen.
But an examiner won't accept don't lift your pen, so we pin it down with three conditions. First, the function must actually exist at the point — f of c has a definite value.
Second, the function must head somewhere definite as you approach. The limit as x tends to c must exist, which needs the approach from the left and from the right to agree.
Written out, the left-hand limit must equal the right-hand limit. If the two sides aim for different heights, you get a jump and the limit simply fails to exist.
Third, the subtle one: where the function is heading must match where it actually lands. The limit has to equal f of c itself.
So the limit as x tends to c equals f of c — one clean equation that quietly packages all three demands into a single test you can apply.
If even one of these fails, the function snaps. A jump when the two sides disagree, a removable hole when they agree but the dot sits somewhere else.
<curious>तो हम किसी function को एक point पर continuous कब कहते हैं? चलिए idea को scratch से बनाते हैं, फिर exam-precise करते हैं।
Socho एक train जिसकी rails बिना किसी gap के जुड़ी हैं। सफर smoothly चलता रहता है। यही unbroken path continuity है — आप pen उठाए बिना graph बनाते हैं।
But examiner को 'pen मत उठाओ' नहीं चलेगा, तो हम इसे three conditions से pin करते हैं। पहली, function उस point पर exist करे — f of c की एक definite value हो।
दूसरी, approach करते हुए function किसी definite जगह जाए। limit as x tends to c exist करे, यानी left और right से approach दोनों agree करें।
यानी left hand limit, right hand limit के बराबर हो। अगर दोनों sides अलग height पर जाएं तो jump बनता है और limit exist ही नहीं करती।
तीसरी, subtle वाली: function जहां जा रहा है वहीं land भी करे। limit को f of c के equal होना चाहिए।
तो limit as x tends to c equals f of c — एक clean equation जो तीनों demands को एक ही test में pack कर देती है।
अगर एक भी fail हो, function snap कर जाता है। Sides disagree करें तो jump, agree करें पर dot कहीं और हो तो removable hole।

sections.title: Differentiability and the one-way bridge

board_events.text: Differentiability = smoothness, a stronger demand
Smooth road: one well-defined direction at every instant.
Sharp hairpin: no single direction at the kink — not differentiable.

board_events.text: The single most important relationship
But continuous does NOT imply differentiable — the arrow runs one way.
Smoothness fails at: corners (|x|), cusps or vertical tangents ($x^{1/3}$ at $0$), and every discontinuity.

segments.text: Continuity only asks that the graph be unbroken. Differentiability asks for something stronger — that the graph be smooth, with no sharp corners anywhere.
Think of a long, gently banked expressway curve. You keep the wheel turning smoothly, and at every instant there is exactly one direction you are pointing. That is a differentiable path.

Now a sharp hairpin in the Ghats that suddenly kinks. At the corner there is no single direction — you point one way an instant before and another way after. That corner is non-differentiable, even though the road never broke.

The classic mathematical hairpin is the absolute value function at zero. The graph is a perfect V: unbroken, but at the tip the slope is minus one coming in and plus one going out. No single tangent, so continuous but not differentiable.
This gives us the most important sentence in the whole subtopic, and examiners test it relentlessly, so lock it in now.
<whisper>Differentiability is strictly stronger than continuity. Every differentiable function is continuous — smooth implies unbroken.
The reverse is false. A continuous function need not be differentiable — the V is unbroken yet cornered. Memorise the direction of that arrow; it only runs one way.

Smoothness can fail three ways: a corner like the V, a cusp or vertical tangent like the cube root at zero where the slope blows up, and anywhere the function is already broken — a break kills smoothness automatically.
Continuity सिर्फ यह माँगती है कि graph unbroken हो। Differentiability इससे strong माँग करती है — graph smooth हो, कहीं कोई sharp corner न हो।
Socho expressway का एक long, gently banked curve. आप wheel smoothly घुमाते रहते हैं, और हर instant पर exactly एक direction होती है। यही differentiable path है।
अब Ghats का एक sharp hairpin जो अचानक kink करता है। corner पर कोई single direction नहीं — एक instant पहले एक तरफ, बाद में दूसरी तरफ। वो corner non-differentiable है, चाहे road टूटी नहीं।

Classic mathematical hairpin है absolute value function, zero पर। graph एक perfect V है: unbroken, पर tip पर slope minus one आते हुए और plus one जाते हुए। कोई single tangent नहीं, तो continuous but not differentiable।
यहाँ से पूरे subtopic का सबसे important sentence मिलता है, और examiners इसे बार-बार test करते हैं, तो इसे अभी lock कर लो।
<whisper>Differentiability, continuity से strictly strong है। हर differentiable function continuous होता है — smooth implies unbroken।
Reverse false है। continuous function differentiable होना ज़रूरी नहीं — V unbroken है पर cornered। उस arrow की direction याद रखो; यह सिर्फ एक तरफ चलती है।

Smoothness तीन तरह fail होती है: corner जैसे V, cusp या vertical tangent जैसे cube root zero पर जहाँ slope infinity हो जाती है, और कहीं भी जहाँ function पहले से broken है — break smoothness अपने आप kill कर देता है।

sections.title: Precise definitions: LHL, RHL, LHD, RHD

board_events.text: The pointwise definitions you compute with
Bridge theorem: differentiable at $c$ $\Rightarrow$ continuous at $c$. The converse is false.
Strategy: for piecewise functions, only the junction points are doubtful — always check continuity BEFORE differentiability.

segments.text: Let's collect the exact machinery you actually compute with. Everything reduces to left-hand and right-hand quantities built with a small positive step h.
Continuity at c in one line: the limit equals the value, which unpacks to left-hand limit equals right-hand limit equals f of c. All three tied together.
Writing h tending to zero from the positive side, the left-hand limit uses c minus h, and the right-hand limit uses c plus h. Same little h, approached from the two sides.
Differentiability at c means this single limit — the difference quotient — exists and is finite. That is the instantaneous slope, the derivative at the point.
It splits into one-sided derivatives. The left-hand derivative uses the left piece, with the step being minus h in the denominator because you moved backward.
The right-hand derivative uses the right piece with an ordinary plus h step. Differentiable at c means these two are equal and both finite.
And the bridge theorem sits on top: if the derivative exists at c, continuity there is guaranteed. The converse fails, as the V reminds us.

Practical takeaway: for a piecewise function only the junction points are doubtful; standard pieces are automatically smooth. And always test continuity first — if it fails, differentiability cannot hold, so you stop.
चलिए exact machinery collect करते हैं जिससे आप actually compute करते हो। सब कुछ left hand और right hand quantities में reduce होता है, जो एक small positive step h से बनती हैं।
Continuity at c एक line में: limit equals value, जो unpack होता है left hand limit equals right hand limit equals f of c में। तीनों एक साथ बंधे।
h को positive side से zero की तरफ लेते हुए, left hand limit c minus h use करती है, right hand limit c plus h। वही little h, दोनों sides से approach।
Differentiability at c का मतलब है यह single limit — difference quotient — exist करे और finite हो। यही instantaneous slope है, point पर derivative।
यह one-sided derivatives में split होती है। left hand derivative left piece use करती है, denominator में minus h क्योंकि आप backward गए।
right hand derivative right piece use करती है, ordinary plus h step के साथ। differentiable at c का मतलब ये दोनों equal हों और both finite।
और ऊपर bridge theorem: अगर derivative c पर exist करे, तो continuity guaranteed है। converse fail होता है, जैसा V याद दिलाता है।

Practical takeaway: piecewise function में सिर्फ junction points doubtful हैं; standard pieces अपने आप smooth हैं। और हमेशा continuity पहले test करो — fail हुई तो differentiability हो ही नहीं सकती, तो रुक जाओ।

sections.title: Proof: differentiable implies continuous

board_events.text: Board proof: differentiable at $c$ $\Rightarrow$ continuous at $c$
Given: $f'(c)$ exists. Want: $\lim_{x\to c}\,[f(x) - f(c)] = 0$.
The right side is now a product of two pieces whose limits we already know.
Therefore $\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = f(c)$ — that is continuity at $c$.
Why the converse fails: we needed $f'(c)$ finite. For $|x|$ at $0$ it doesn't exist, so the argument collapses.

segments.text: Here is the one proof from this subtopic that genuinely shows up in Boards, and the reasoning is elegant. We assume the derivative exists and squeeze out continuity.
We are given f dash c exists, a finite number. We want to show the limit of f of x minus f of c is zero, because that is exactly continuity restated.
The key algebraic trick: multiply and divide by x minus c. For x not equal to c this factor is non-zero, so we have changed absolutely nothing.
Why bother? Because the right side is now a product of two pieces we understand. The first is the difference quotient, the second is just x minus c.
Take the limit using the product rule for limits, valid because both limits exist and are finite. The first factor goes to f dash c, the second goes to zero, and the product is zero.
So the limit of f of x minus f of c is zero, which means the limit of f of x equals f of c. That is precisely continuity at c. Proof complete.

Notice we needed f dash c to exist for the first factor to have a finite limit. For the V at zero it does not exist, the argument collapses, and indeed the V is continuous without being differentiable. The arrow runs one way only.
यह वो एक proof है जो सच में Boards में आता है, और reasoning elegant है। हम मानते हैं derivative exist करती है और continuity निकाल लेते हैं।
हमें दिया है f dash c exist करती है, एक finite number। हमें दिखाना है कि limit of f of x minus f of c zero है, क्योंकि यही continuity को restate करता है।
Key algebraic trick: x minus c से multiply और divide करो। x not equal to c के लिए यह factor non-zero है, तो हमने कुछ भी नहीं बदला।
फ़ायदा क्या? क्योंकि right side अब दो pieces का product है जिन्हें हम समझते हैं। पहला difference quotient, दूसरा सिर्फ x minus c।
product rule for limits से limit लो, valid क्योंकि दोनों limits exist और finite हैं। पहला factor f dash c पर जाता है, दूसरा zero पर, और product zero।
तो limit of f of x minus f of c zero है, यानी limit of f of x equals f of c। यही exactly continuity at c है। Proof complete।

ध्यान दो, पहले factor की finite limit के लिए f dash c का exist करना ज़रूरी था। V के लिए zero पर यह exist नहीं करती, argument collapse हो जाता है, और सच में V continuous है but differentiable नहीं। arrow सिर्फ एक तरफ।

sections.title: Making a piecewise function continuous — find k

board_events.text: Find $k$ so the piecewise function is continuous at $x = 2$
For $k = 4$ the two pieces meet at height $7$ — continuous at $x = 2$.

segments.text: A Board-favourite: we are handed a piecewise function and asked to choose the constant k that stitches the two pieces together continuously at the junction x equals two.
The first piece is two x plus three for x up to and including two, and the second is k x minus one beyond two. Only the junction is doubtful.
Step one, the value at the point. Since x equals two belongs to the first piece, f of two is two times two plus three, which is seven.
Step two, the left-hand limit. Approaching from below we still use the first piece, so the left-hand limit is also seven. So far, so consistent.
Step three, the right-hand limit. Approaching from above uses the second piece, giving two k minus one — and here the unknown k finally enters.
Step four, impose continuity: the right-hand limit must equal the value seven. So two k minus one equals seven, giving two k equals eight, hence k equals four.
So for k equal to four the two pieces meet at the common height seven, and the function is continuous at x equals two. That single equation did all the work.
Board का favourite: हमें एक piecewise function दिया है और k वो constant चुनना है जो दोनों pieces को junction x equals two पर continuously जोड़ दे।
पहला piece है two x plus three, x up to and including two के लिए, और दूसरा k x minus one, two के आगे। सिर्फ junction doubtful है।
Step one, point पर value। चूँकि x equals two पहले piece में है, f of two होता है two times two plus three, यानी seven।
Step two, left hand limit। नीचे से approach करते हुए हम पहला piece use करते हैं, तो left hand limit भी seven है। अब तक consistent।
Step three, right hand limit। ऊपर से approach दूसरा piece use करता है, देता है two k minus one — और यहाँ unknown k आख़िरकार आता है।
Step four, continuity impose करो: right hand limit value seven के equal हो। तो two k minus one equals seven, यानी two k equals eight, hence k equals four।
तो k equal to four के लिए दोनों pieces common height seven पर मिलते हैं, और function x equals two पर continuous है। उस एक equation ने सारा काम कर दिया।

board_events.text: LHD $= 4 \neq 3 =$ RHD $\Rightarrow$ not differentiable at $x = 2$, though continuous.

segments.text: Now a JEE-Main level classic: the same piecewise idea, but we push past continuity into differentiability and watch the bridge theorem bite.
The left piece is x squared, the right piece is three x minus two, joining at x equals two. First continuity, then the derivatives.
Continuity is clean. The value is four, the left-hand limit from x squared is four, the right-hand limit from three x minus two is also four. All agree, so continuous at two.
Now the one-sided derivatives. The left-hand derivative uses x squared: expand two minus h squared minus four, divide by minus h, simplify, and the limit is four.
The right-hand derivative uses three x minus two: the numerator collapses to three h, divided by h gives three. So the right slope is three.
Picture it: the parabola arrives at the point two comma four with slope four, but the line leaves with slope three. Different slopes, so the graph has a corner right at the join.
Since four is not equal to three, the function is not differentiable at two — yet it is continuous there. This is the bridge theorem in action: continuity does not buy you smoothness.
अब एक JEE Main level classic: वही piecewise idea, पर हम continuity से आगे differentiability में जाते हैं और bridge theorem को काम करते देखते हैं।
Left piece x squared, right piece three x minus two, x equals two पर जुड़ते हैं। पहले continuity, फिर derivatives।
Continuity clean है। value four, x squared से left hand limit four, three x minus two से right hand limit भी four। सब agree, तो two पर continuous।
अब one-sided derivatives। left hand derivative x squared use करती है: two minus h squared minus four expand करो, minus h से divide, simplify, और limit four है।
right hand derivative three x minus two use करती है: numerator three h में collapse होता है, h से divide करने पर three। तो right slope three है।
इसे picture करो: parabola point two comma four पर slope four से आती है, पर line slope three से जाती है। अलग slopes, तो graph में join पर corner है।
चूँकि four, three के equal नहीं, function two पर differentiable नहीं — फिर भी वहाँ continuous है। यही bridge theorem action में है: continuity smoothness नहीं ख़रीदती।

sections.title: Counting non-differentiable points of a modulus sum

board_events.text: How many points is $f(x) = |x^{2}-4| + |x-1|$ non-differentiable?
A term $|g(x)|$ makes a corner exactly where $g(x)$ crosses zero AND changes sign.
The trap: $x = 0$ is the vertex of $x^{2}-4$, but the inside stays negative there — no sign change, no corner.
Adding functions smooths a kink only if both kink at the same place — here $-2, 1, 2$ are distinct.

segments.text: <curious>A JEE speed-trap. Two temptations mislead students: rushing to differentiate, or assuming each modulus contributes exactly one kink. Both go wrong.
The fast rule: a modulus of g creates a corner exactly where g equals zero and changes sign. Everywhere else it is perfectly smooth, including where the inside just touches its own vertex.
The first term, x squared minus four, is zero at minus two and at two, and it changes sign at both. So that term alone gives two corners.
The second term, x minus one, is zero and sign-changing at just one place, x equals one. That is one more corner.

Here is the classic blunder: also counting x equals zero, the vertex of x squared minus four. But near zero the inside stays negative, so the modulus is just four minus x squared, perfectly smooth. No sign change, no corner.
Could the sum accidentally smooth a kink? Only if both terms cornered at the same point. Here the corners sit at distinct places, minus two, one, and two, so all three survive the addition.
So the answer is three points: minus two, one, and two. Count sign-changes of the inside, never zeros of its derivative — that distinction is the whole game here.
<curious>एक JEE speed-trap। दो temptations गुमराह करती हैं: differentiate करने की जल्दी, या यह मानना कि हर modulus exactly एक kink देता है। दोनों ग़लत।
Fast rule: modulus of g वहीं corner बनाता है जहाँ g zero हो और sign बदले। बाक़ी हर जगह वो perfectly smooth है, उस point पर भी जहाँ inside सिर्फ अपने vertex को touch करता है।
पहला term, x squared minus four, minus two और two पर zero है, और दोनों पर sign बदलता है। तो अकेला यह term two corners देता है।
दूसरा term, x minus one, सिर्फ एक जगह zero और sign-changing है, x equals one। यह एक और corner।

यहाँ classic blunder: x equals zero को भी count करना, जो x squared minus four का vertex है। पर zero के पास inside negative ही रहता है, तो modulus सिर्फ four minus x squared है, perfectly smooth। कोई sign change नहीं, कोई corner नहीं।
क्या sum गलती से kink smooth कर सकता है? सिर्फ तब जब दोनों terms एक ही point पर corner करें। यहाँ corners अलग जगहों पर हैं, minus two, one, two, तो तीनों addition के बाद survive करते हैं।
तो answer तीन points: minus two, one, two। inside के sign-changes count करो, कभी उसके derivative के zeros नहीं — यही distinction पूरा खेल है।

sections.title: The gem: differentiable with a discontinuous derivative

board_events.text: Differentiable everywhere, yet $f'$ is not continuous at $0$
As $x \to 0$: the first term $\to 0$, but $\cos\frac{1}{x}$ oscillates forever — no limit.
$f'(0) = 0$ exists, yet $\lim_{x\to 0} f'(x)$ does not — $f'$ is discontinuous at $0$.

segments.text: <excited>Now the gem of the subtopic — a JEE Advanced favourite. A function that is differentiable at zero, and yet its own derivative is not even continuous there.
The function is x squared times sine of one over x away from zero, and defined to be zero at the origin. The sine part oscillates wildly, but the x squared tames it.
Step one, continuity by the squeeze theorem. Since sine is bounded by one, the whole thing is trapped between zero and x squared, which goes to zero. So the limit is zero, matching f of zero.

Step two, differentiability at zero from first principles. The difference quotient simplifies to h times sine of one over h, again squeezed to zero. So the derivative at the origin exists and equals zero.
Step three, the derivative away from zero, using product and chain rules. It comes out as two x sine one over x minus cosine one over x. Keep an eye on that second term.

Step four, is the derivative continuous at zero? The first term is squeezed to zero, but cosine of one over x oscillates between minus one and one infinitely often as x approaches zero. It has no limit.

So the derivative at zero exists and is zero, yet the limit of the derivative does not exist. The derivative is discontinuous at zero. Differentiability does not force the derivative to be continuous — the fact that separates memorising from understanding.
<excited>अब subtopic का gem — JEE Advanced favourite। एक function जो zero पर differentiable है, फिर भी उसका अपना derivative वहाँ continuous तक नहीं।
Function है x squared times sine of one over x, zero से दूर, और origin पर zero define किया है। sine part wildly oscillate करता है, पर x squared उसे tame कर देता है।
Step one, squeeze theorem से continuity। चूँकि sine one से bounded है, पूरी चीज़ zero और x squared के बीच trapped है, जो zero पर जाता है। तो limit zero है, f of zero से match।
Step two, zero पर differentiability first principles से। difference quotient h times sine of one over h में simplify होता है, फिर squeeze होकर zero। तो origin पर derivative exist करती है और zero है।
Step three, zero से दूर derivative, product और chain rules से। यह निकलता है two x sine one over x minus cosine one over x। उस दूसरे term पर नज़र रखो।

Step four, क्या derivative zero पर continuous है? पहला term zero पर squeeze हो जाता है, पर cosine of one over x, x के zero पर पहुँचते ही minus one और one के बीच infinitely oscillate करता है। इसकी कोई limit नहीं।

तो zero पर derivative exist करती है और zero है, फिर भी derivative की limit exist नहीं करती। derivative zero पर discontinuous है। Differentiability, derivative को continuous होने पर मजबूर नहीं करती — यही fact memorising और understanding को अलग करता है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: continuity and differentiability

board_events.text: The four traps that cost marks here
Trap 1: believing continuous $\Rightarrow$ differentiable. It is the other way round.
Trap 2: skipping the continuity check before computing LHD and RHD.
Trap 3: miscounting modulus corners — count sign-changes of the inside, not zeros of its derivative.
Trap 4: over-counting endpoints in open intervals like $(0,3)$.
Mnemonic — DiCo, not CoDi: Differentiable $\Rightarrow$ Continuous, but Continuous does not $\Rightarrow$ Differentiable.

segments.text: Let's bank the mistakes that quietly cost marks in this subtopic, and the habits that immunise you against them.
Trap one, the reversed arrow. Believing continuous implies differentiable. It is the other way round. Keep the V at zero in your pocket as the eternal counterexample.

Trap two, skipping the continuity check. If the function is already discontinuous at the point, it cannot be differentiable, and grinding out one-sided derivatives just wastes time and can hand you a misleading finite number.
Trap three, miscounting modulus corners. Do not treat every modulus as one corner, and do not count a vertex where the inside never changes sign. Count sign-changes of the inside function.
Trap four, endpoint over-counting. In an open interval, the endpoints are excluded, so a kink or jump sitting exactly on the boundary does not count toward your tally.

The master pro-tip: for piecewise functions test only the junction points, never the smooth interiors, and always run continuity first, differentiability second. The first failure instantly settles the question.
And a mnemonic to carry into the exam hall: DiCo, not CoDi. Differentiable implies Continuous, but Continuous does not imply Differentiable. Four syllables, one whole theorem.
चलिए वो mistakes bank करते हैं जो इस subtopic में चुपचाप marks खा जाती हैं, और वो habits जो आपको इनसे बचाती हैं।
Trap one, reversed arrow। यह मानना कि continuous implies differentiable। यह उल्टा है। V को zero पर अपनी जेब में रखो, eternal counterexample की तरह।

Trap two, continuity check skip करना। अगर function point पर पहले से discontinuous है, वो differentiable हो ही नहीं सकता, और one-sided derivatives निकालना सिर्फ time waste करता है और misleading finite number दे सकता है।
Trap three, modulus corners miscount करना। हर modulus को एक corner मत मानो, और उस vertex को count मत करो जहाँ inside sign नहीं बदलता। inside function के sign-changes count करो।
Trap four, endpoint over-counting। open interval में endpoints excluded हैं, तो boundary पर बैठा kink या jump आपकी गिनती में नहीं आता।
Master pro-tip: piecewise functions में सिर्फ junction points test करो, कभी smooth interiors नहीं, और हमेशा continuity पहले, differentiability बाद में। पहला failure तुरंत सवाल settle कर देता है।
और exam hall में ले जाने के लिए mnemonic: DiCo, not CoDi। Differentiable implies Continuous, but Continuous does not imply Differentiable। चार syllables, एक पूरा theorem।

board_events.text: Two things you need to differentiate anything
The spice rack = standard derivatives; the techniques = sum, product, quotient rules.
The most seductive mistake: guessing $(uv)' = u'v'$.

board_events.caption: Growing a rectangle of area uv: a top strip u·dv plus a side strip v·du

board_events.text: Top strip = $u\,dv$; side strip = $v\,du$. The new area gains BOTH.
A one-term answer to a product is wrong by inspection — you always owe two strips.

segments.text: Learning to differentiate is a lot like learning to cook. You need two things: a spice rack of standard ingredients you know cold, and a few techniques to combine them.
The spice rack is the list of standard derivatives — sine, e to the x, x to the n. The techniques are the rules for a sum, a product, a quotient. Master both and almost nothing can stop you.

The standard derivatives are just facts to memorise. The rules are where intuition matters — and the most seductive mistake in all of calculus is guessing that the derivative of a product is the product of the derivatives.
Picture a rectangle with width u and height v, so its area is u times v. Now nudge both sides up a little. The area grows by a thin strip along the top and a thin strip along the side.
The top strip comes from the height growing, that is u times dv. The side strip comes from the width growing, that is v times du. The new area gains both strips, not one.
That picture is the product rule: u dash v plus u v dash. And it is exactly why the naive guess fails — it quietly forgets one of the two strips.
Bank this as a reflex: a product's derivative has two terms. A single-term answer to a product is wrong just by looking at it. You always owe both strips.
Differentiate सीखना cooking सीखने जैसा है। आपको दो चीज़ें चाहिए: standard ingredients का एक spice rack जो आपको रट्टा हो, और उन्हें combine करने की कुछ techniques।
spice rack है standard derivatives की list — sine, e to the x, x to the n। techniques हैं sum, product, quotient के rules। दोनों में महारत, तो कुछ नहीं रोक सकता।

standard derivatives सिर्फ facts हैं जो रटने हैं। rules वहाँ हैं जहाँ intuition matters — और पूरे calculus की सबसे seductive mistake है यह guess करना कि product का derivative, derivatives का product है।
Socho एक rectangle जिसकी width u और height v है, तो area u times v। अब दोनों sides को थोड़ा बढ़ाओ। area बढ़ता है top के एक thin strip और side के एक thin strip से।
top strip height बढ़ने से आता है, यानी u times dv। side strip width बढ़ने से, यानी v times du। नया area दोनों strips पाता है, एक नहीं।
वो picture ही product rule है: u dash v plus u v dash। और यही वजह है naive guess fail होता है — वो चुपचाप दो में से एक strip भूल जाता है।
इसे reflex बना लो: product के derivative के दो terms होते हैं। product का single-term answer देखते ही ग़लत है। आप हमेशा दोनों strips के क़र्ज़दार हो।

sections.subtopic: The Differentiation Toolkit — Standard Derivatives & Rules
sections.title: The algebra of continuous functions

board_events.text: Why standard functions are continuous everywhere
If $f$ and $g$ are continuous at $c$, so are $f+g$, $f-g$, and $fg$.
The quotient $f/g$ is continuous at $c$ provided $g(c) \neq 0$.
The composite $f(g(x))$ is continuous if $g$ is continuous at $c$ and $f$ at $g(c)$.
So polynomials, $\sin x$, $\cos x$, $e^{x}$ and sensible combinations are continuous on their domains.
This is why only piecewise junctions ever need checking — the smooth interiors are guaranteed.
Validity: the quotient rule needs $v \neq 0$; each standard derivative holds only on its own domain.

segments.text: There is a quieter idea hiding in the toolkit that explains a puzzle from the foundations: why we only ever checked junction points and trusted the smooth interiors.
The principle is this. If f and g are both continuous at a point, then their sum, their difference, and their product are all continuous there too. Continuity is preserved under these operations.
The quotient f over g is also continuous, but with one caveat: the denominator must be non-zero at the point. Divide by zero and continuity breaks, as one over x reminds us at the origin.
And composites are continuous too: if g is continuous at c and f is continuous at g of c, then f of g of x is continuous at c. Chaining continuous functions keeps you continuous.

This is exactly why polynomials, sine, cosine, e to the x, and all their sensible combinations are continuous wherever they are defined. They are built from continuous pieces by continuity-preserving operations.

And that closes the loop with the foundations: it is precisely why, for piecewise functions, only the suspicious junctions need checking. The smooth interiors are guaranteed continuous by this algebra.

One validity note to carry forward: the quotient rule needs the denominator non-zero, and each standard derivative holds only on its natural domain — log needs x positive, inverse secant needs magnitude of x above one.
toolkit में एक शांत idea छिपा है जो foundations की एक पहेली समझाता है: हमने सिर्फ junction points क्यों check किए और smooth interiors पर भरोसा किया।
Principle यह है। अगर f और g दोनों एक point पर continuous हैं, तो उनका sum, difference, और product सब वहाँ continuous हैं। इन operations में continuity preserve होती है।
quotient f over g भी continuous है, पर एक caveat के साथ: denominator point पर non-zero हो। zero से divide करो और continuity टूटती है, जैसा one over x origin पर याद दिलाता है।
और composites भी continuous हैं: अगर g, c पर continuous और f, g of c पर continuous, तो f of g of x, c पर continuous। continuous functions को chain करना continuous ही रखता है।
यही वजह है polynomials, sine, cosine, e to the x, और उनके सब sensible combinations जहाँ define हैं वहाँ continuous हैं। वे continuous pieces से continuity-preserving operations द्वारा बने हैं।
और यह foundations के साथ loop बंद करता है: यही exact वजह है कि piecewise functions में सिर्फ suspicious junctions check करने होते हैं। smooth interiors इस algebra से guaranteed continuous हैं।

एक validity note आगे के लिए: quotient rule को denominator non-zero चाहिए, और हर standard derivative सिर्फ अपने natural domain पर valid है — log को x positive चाहिए, inverse secant को magnitude of x, one से ऊपर।

sections.subtopic: The Differentiation Toolkit — Standard Derivatives & Rules
sections.title: The standard-derivatives table

board_events.text: The spice rack, laid out

board_events.latex: \frac{d}{dx}\cot x = -\csc^{2}x, \quad \frac{d}{dx}\sec x = \sec x\tan x, \quad \frac{d}{dx}\csc x = -\csc x\cot x

board_events.text: Cofunctions ($\cos^{-1}, \cot^{-1}, \csc^{-1}$) match magnitudes but carry a minus sign.

segments.text: Here is the spice rack itself — the standard derivatives you must recall instantly. Each holds on its natural domain. Let's walk the shelves.
The power rule: x to the n differentiates to n times x to the n minus one. And any constant differentiates to zero — flat lines have no slope.
The core trig trio: sine goes to cosine, cosine goes to minus sine — mind that negative — and tangent goes to secant squared.
The reciprocal trio: cotangent to minus cosecant squared, secant to secant tan, cosecant to minus cosecant cot. Notice cotangent and cosecant carry a minus sign.
The exponential and log shelf: e to the x is its own derivative, its party trick. A general a to the x picks up a natural-log-of-a factor, and natural log of x gives one over x.
Two headline inverse-trig results, which we will derive properly in a later part: inverse sine gives one over root one minus x squared, and inverse tan gives one over one plus x squared.
And a memory hook for the rest: the cofunctions — inverse cosine, inverse cotangent, inverse cosecant — have the same magnitude as their partners but carry a minus sign in front.
यह रहा spice rack — वो standard derivatives जो तुरंत याद होने चाहिए। हर एक अपने natural domain पर valid है। चलिए shelves पर चलते हैं।
Power rule: x to the n, differentiate होकर n times x to the n minus one। और कोई भी constant zero देता है — flat lines की कोई slope नहीं।
Core trig trio: sine जाता है cosine, cosine जाता है minus sine — उस negative का ध्यान — और tangent जाता है secant squared।
Reciprocal trio: cotangent जाता है minus cosecant squared, secant जाता है secant tan, cosecant जाता है minus cosecant cot। ध्यान दो cotangent और cosecant minus sign रखते हैं।
Exponential और log shelf: e to the x अपना ही derivative है, इसका party trick। general a to the x एक natural log of a factor उठाता है, और natural log of x देता है one over x।
दो headline inverse-trig results, जिन्हें हम बाद के part में ठीक से derive करेंगे: inverse sine देता है one over root one minus x squared, और inverse tan देता है one over one plus x squared।
और बाक़ी के लिए एक memory hook: cofunctions — inverse cosine, inverse cotangent, inverse cosecant — अपने partners जैसी ही magnitude रखते हैं पर आगे minus sign लगाते हैं।

sections.subtopic: The Differentiation Toolkit — Standard Derivatives & Rules
sections.title: The rules of differentiation

board_events.text: How to combine the ingredients
Order matters: it is $u'v - uv'$, never $uv' - u'v$.
Mnemonic (quotient): low d-high minus high d-low, over low-squared.

segments.text: With the spice rack stocked, here are the combining techniques — the rules that let you differentiate sums, products, and quotients built from those ingredients.
The sum and difference rule is the friendly one: differentiate term by term. The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives — here the naive instinct is actually correct.
The constant-multiple rule: a constant just rides along outside. Differentiate the function and keep the constant sitting in front, untouched.
The product rule, our rectangle made rigorous: u dash v plus u v dash. Two terms, always. This is the one the naive guess gets wrong.
The quotient rule: low d-high minus high d-low, all over low squared. The order matters enormously — u dash v comes first, then minus u v dash, and the denominator is v squared.
Do not flip that numerator. It is u dash v minus u v dash, never the other way. Swapping the order silently negates your whole answer — the single most common quotient-rule sign error.
The rhyme that saves you under pressure: low d-high minus high d-low, over low-squared. Chant it, and the order fixes itself every single time.
spice rack भर गया, अब combining techniques — वो rules जो आपको उन ingredients से बने sums, products, और quotients differentiate करने देते हैं।
Sum और difference rule सबसे friendly है: term by term differentiate करो। sum का derivative, derivatives का sum है — यहाँ naive instinct सच में सही है।
Constant-multiple rule: constant बस बाहर साथ चलता है। function differentiate करो और constant को आगे बैठा रहने दो, untouched।
Product rule, हमारा rectangle rigorous रूप में: u dash v plus u v dash। दो terms, हमेशा। यही वो है जिसे naive guess ग़लत करता है।
Quotient rule: low d-high minus high d-low, सब low squared के ऊपर। order बहुत matter करता है — u dash v पहले, फिर minus u v dash, और denominator v squared।
उस numerator को flip मत करो। यह u dash v minus u v dash है, कभी उल्टा नहीं। order swap करना चुपचाप पूरा answer negate कर देता है — सबसे common quotient-rule sign error।
Pressure में बचाने वाली rhyme: low d-high minus high d-low, over low-squared। इसे बोलो, और order हर बार अपने आप सही हो जाएगा।

sections.subtopic: The Differentiation Toolkit — Standard Derivatives & Rules
sections.title: First-principles: deriving sine and the product rule

board_events.text: Where two spice-rack facts actually come from
Add-and-subtract, then split into two limits $\Rightarrow (uv)' = u'v + uv'$.

segments.text: We derive a couple of these so you trust the rack rather than just memorising it. First the derivative of sine, then the product rule itself.
Start from first principles with f equal to sine x. The difference quotient is sine of x plus h minus sine x, all over h.
Apply the identity sine C minus sine D equals two cosine of the half-sum times sine of the half-difference. The numerator becomes two cosine of x plus h over two, times sine of h over two.
Regroup so the second factor is sine of h over two divided by h over two. That is the famous limit — sine theta over theta tends to one — and the first factor tends to cosine x.
The famous limit gives one, the first factor gives cosine x, so the derivative of sine is cosine. The spice-rack fact, earned rather than assumed.
Now the product rule. Start from the difference quotient of u times v. The trick is to subtract and add u of x plus h times v of x in the numerator — it changes nothing but lets us factor.
After that add-and-subtract, the numerator splits into two groups. Taking the limit, each group becomes one strip: you land exactly on u dash v plus u v dash. The two rectangle strips, made rigorous.
हम इनमें से कुछ derive करते हैं ताकि आप rack पर भरोसा करो, सिर्फ रटो नहीं। पहले sine का derivative, फिर product rule ख़ुद।
First principles से शुरू करो, f equal to sine x। difference quotient है sine of x plus h minus sine x, सब h के ऊपर।
Identity लगाओ: sine C minus sine D equals two cosine of half-sum times sine of half-difference। numerator बनता है two cosine of x plus h over two, times sine of h over two।
Regroup करो ताकि दूसरा factor sine of h over two divided by h over two बने। यही famous limit है — sine theta over theta, one पर जाता है — और पहला factor cosine x पर।
famous limit one देती है, पहला factor cosine x, तो sine का derivative cosine है। spice-rack fact, माना नहीं, कमाया।
अब product rule। u times v के difference quotient से शुरू। trick है numerator में u of x plus h times v of x subtract और add करना — बदलता कुछ नहीं पर factor करने देता है।
उस add-and-subtract के बाद, numerator दो groups में split होता है। limit लेने पर हर group एक strip बनता है: आप exactly u dash v plus u v dash पर पहुँचते हो। rectangle के दो strips, rigorous रूप में।

sections.subtopic: The Differentiation Toolkit — Standard Derivatives & Rules
sections.title: Product and quotient rules in action

board_events.text: Two clean applications

board_events.latex: y' = \frac{\cos x(1+\cos x) - \sin x(-\sin x)}{(1+\cos x)^{2}}

segments.text: Now the rules on real functions — one product, one quotient — with a lovely simplification hiding in the second one.
First, differentiate y equal to x squared plus one, times x cubed plus three. Set u as the first bracket and v as the second, then reach for the product rule.
u dash is two x, v dash is three x squared. So y dash is two x times the second bracket, plus the first bracket times three x squared. Two terms, as a product demands.
Expand and collect like terms and it tidies to five x to the fourth, plus three x squared, plus six x. Clean.
Second, a quotient: y equal to sine x over one plus cosine x. Quotient rule with u as sine x and v as one plus cosine x.
Low d-high minus high d-low: cosine x times one plus cosine x, minus sine x times minus sine x, all over one plus cosine x squared. Watch that double negative become a plus.
The Pythagorean identity collapses the numerator to one plus cosine x, which cancels one factor downstairs, leaving simply one over one plus cosine x. Always look for that simplification.
अब असली functions पर rules — एक product, एक quotient — और दूसरे में एक प्यारी simplification छिपी है।
पहले, y equal to x squared plus one, times x cubed plus three differentiate करो। u को पहला bracket, v को दूसरा मानो, फिर product rule।
u dash है two x, v dash है three x squared। तो y dash है two x times दूसरा bracket, plus पहला bracket times three x squared। दो terms, जैसा product माँगता है।
Expand करो और like terms collect करो, यह five x to the fourth, plus three x squared, plus six x में साफ़ हो जाता है। Clean।
दूसरा, एक quotient: y equal to sine x over one plus cosine x। quotient rule, u sine x और v one plus cosine x।
Low d-high minus high d-low: cosine x times one plus cosine x, minus sine x times minus sine x, सब one plus cosine x squared के ऊपर। उस double negative को plus बनते देखो।
Pythagorean identity numerator को one plus cosine x में collapse करती है, जो नीचे एक factor cancel करता है, और बचता है सिर्फ one over one plus cosine x। हमेशा उस simplification को ढूँढो।

sections.subtopic: The Differentiation Toolkit — Standard Derivatives & Rules
sections.title: The (uv)'=u'v' trap, and first principles for 1/√x

board_events.text: Spotting a product error, and a rationalising derivation
A student writes $\frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}\sin x) = 2x\cos x$. Why is that wrong?
The crime: applying the false rule $(uv)' = u'v'$ — multiplying the two derivatives.

board_events.latex: \frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}\sin x) = 2x\sin x + x^{2}\cos x = x(2\sin x + x\cos x)

segments.text: <curious>Two more: first the signature product-rule blunder, then a first-principles derivation that confirms the power rule for a fractional exponent.
A student differentiates x squared sine x and writes two x cosine x. This is the single most common differentiation error — can you see the crime before I say it?
The crime is applying the false rule: multiplying the two derivatives, two x and cosine x, into a single term. That forgets one whole strip of the rectangle.
The fix is the real product rule: two x sine x plus x squared cosine x, which factors as x times the bracket two sine x plus x cosine x. Two terms, exactly as promised.
Now first principles for one over root x. Combine the two fractions in the numerator over a common denominator; you get root x minus root x plus h on top.
Rationalise by multiplying top and bottom by root x plus root x plus h. The numerator becomes x minus x plus h, which is just minus h — and that h cancels the one downstairs.
Let h go to zero and the three root-x factors multiply to two x to the three halves, giving minus one over that. This is exactly the power rule on x to the minus one half. The rack checks out.
<curious>दो और: पहले signature product-rule blunder, फिर एक first-principles derivation जो fractional exponent के लिए power rule confirm करती है।
एक student, x squared sine x differentiate करके two x cosine x लिखता है। यह सबसे common differentiation error है — मेरे बोलने से पहले crime दिख रहा है?
crime है false rule लगाना: दोनों derivatives, two x और cosine x, को एक single term में multiply करना। यह rectangle का एक पूरा strip भूल जाता है।
Fix है असली product rule: two x sine x plus x squared cosine x, जो x times bracket two sine x plus x cosine x में factor होता है। दो terms, बिल्कुल जैसा promise किया।
अब one over root x के लिए first principles। numerator के दो fractions को common denominator पर combine करो; ऊपर मिलता है root x minus root x plus h।
Rationalise करो, top और bottom को root x plus root x plus h से multiply करके। numerator बनता है x minus x plus h, यानी सिर्फ minus h — और वो h नीचे वाले h को cancel करता है।
h को zero जाने दो और तीन root-x factors two x to the three halves में multiply होते हैं, minus one उसके ऊपर देते हैं। यह exactly power rule है x to the minus one half पर। rack सही निकला।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: the differentiation toolkit

board_events.text: Four toolkit traps, and one speed habit
Trap 1: the $(uv)' = u'v'$ trap. A product's derivative has two terms.
Trap 2: flipping the quotient-rule order. It is $u'v - uv'$, not $uv' - u'v$.
Trap 3: trig-derivative sign slips — cos, cot, csc and their inverses all carry a minus.
Trap 4: dropping domain restrictions — $\ln x$ needs $x \gt 0$, $\sec^{-1}x$ carries $|x|$.
Mnemonic: product = two strips; quotient = low d-high minus high d-low, over low-squared.

segments.text: Let's bank the recurring toolkit mistakes and the habit that prevents most of them before they happen.
Trap one, the product trap again, because it never stops appearing. A product's derivative has two terms. A one-term answer to a product is wrong by inspection — no calculation needed.
Trap two, flipping the quotient order. It is u dash v minus u v dash over v squared, never the reverse. Anchor it with low d-high minus high d-low.
Trap three, trig sign slips. Cosine goes to minus sine — that negative is easy to drop. Group the negative ones mentally: cosine, cotangent, cosecant, and their three inverses.
Trap four, dropping domain restrictions. Natural log needs x positive; inverse secant carries an absolute value of x and lives only outside magnitude one. The domain is part of the answer.

The pro-tip that saves the most time: before grinding a quotient, check whether algebra simplifies it first. That sine over one plus cosine example collapsed a messy quotient rule into a one-line answer.
Carry two mnemonics out of here: a product is always two strips, and the quotient rhyme is low d-high minus high d-low, over low-squared. Those two lines cover most toolkit questions.
चलिए recurring toolkit mistakes bank करते हैं और वो habit जो इनमें से ज़्यादातर को होने से पहले रोक देती है।
Trap one, फिर वही product trap, क्योंकि यह कभी आना बंद नहीं होता। product के derivative के दो terms होते हैं। product का one-term answer देखते ही ग़लत — कोई calculation नहीं चाहिए।
Trap two, quotient order flip करना। यह u dash v minus u v dash over v squared है, कभी उल्टा नहीं। इसे low d-high minus high d-low से anchor करो।
Trap three, trig sign slips। cosine जाता है minus sine — वो negative drop करना आसान है। negative वालों को mentally group करो: cosine, cotangent, cosecant, और उनके तीन inverses।
Trap four, domain restrictions drop करना। natural log को x positive चाहिए; inverse secant absolute value of x रखता है और सिर्फ magnitude one के बाहर रहता है। domain answer का हिस्सा है।

सबसे ज़्यादा time बचाने वाला pro-tip: quotient पीसने से पहले देखो कि algebra उसे simplify करती है या नहीं। वो sine over one plus cosine वाला example messy quotient rule को one-line answer में collapse कर देता है।
यहाँ से दो mnemonics ले जाओ: product हमेशा two strips, और quotient rhyme है low d-high minus high d-low, over low-squared। वो दो lines ज़्यादातर toolkit questions cover करती हैं।

board_events.text: A function inside a function
Example: $y = \sin(x^{2})$ means “square it, then take the sine.”

board_events.caption: Rates multiply along the chain: 5 turns per u, 3 u per x, so 15 per x

board_events.text: Recipe: differentiate the OUTER, keep the inner intact, then multiply by the inner's derivative.
Forgetting the $\times\,g'(x)$ factor is the number-one chain-rule error — writing just $\cos(x^{2})$ is wrong.

segments.text: <curious>What happens when one operation is stacked on top of another? That is a composite function, and it needs its own rule to differentiate.
Take y equal to sine of x squared. That is two operations: first square the x, then take the sine of the result. You cannot reach for one single standard derivative here.

The cleanest picture is meshing gears. Turning x drives an intermediate shaft u, which drives the output y. If u spins three times per turn of x, and y spins five times per turn of u, then y spins fifteen times per turn of x.
Rates simply multiply along the chain. The rate of y with respect to x equals the rate of y with respect to u, times the rate of u with respect to x. Five times three is fifteen.
To use it, peel the function like an onion from the outside in. Differentiate the outer function while keeping the inner part untouched, then multiply by the derivative of the inner part.
For sine of x squared: the outer sine differentiates to cosine, evaluated at the untouched inner x squared. Then multiply by the inner derivative two x. The answer is two x cosine of x squared.
That final multiply-by-the-inside is the entire trick, and forgetting it is the number-one chain-rule error. Writing cosine of x squared and stopping is wrong — you still owe the extra factor two x.
<curious>क्या होता है जब एक operation दूसरे के ऊपर stack हो जाए? यही composite function है, और इसे differentiate करने के लिए अपना rule चाहिए।
y equal to sine of x squared लो। यह दो operations हैं: पहले x को square करो, फिर result का sine लो। यहाँ एक single standard derivative काम नहीं आएगा।

सबसे clean picture है meshing gears। x घुमाने से intermediate shaft u चलता है, जो output y चलाता है। अगर u, x के हर turn पर तीन बार घूमे, और y, u के हर turn पर पाँच बार, तो y, x के हर turn पर पंद्रह बार घूमेगा।
Rates बस chain के साथ multiply होती हैं। rate of y with respect to x equals rate of y with respect to u, times rate of u with respect to x। पाँच times three is fifteen।
इसे use करने के लिए, function को प्याज़ की तरह बाहर से अंदर छीलो। outer function differentiate करो, inner part को untouched रखते हुए, फिर inner part के derivative से multiply करो।
sine of x squared के लिए: outer sine, cosine में differentiate होता है, untouched inner x squared पर evaluate। फिर inner derivative two x से multiply। answer है two x cosine of x squared।
वो आख़िरी multiply-by-the-inside ही पूरा trick है, और इसे भूलना नंबर-वन chain-rule error है। cosine of x squared लिखकर रुक जाना ग़लत है — आप पर अभी भी extra factor two x का क़र्ज़ है।

sections.title: The chain rule and its common patterns

board_events.text: Two links, and as many as you like

board_events.latex: y = f(u),\; u = g(x) \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dy}{dx} = f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x)

board_events.text: Validity: $g$ differentiable at $x$, and $f$ differentiable at $u = g(x)$; both links must hold.

segments.text: Let's state the rule precisely, then the extended form for deeper nesting, then the patterns you will reuse constantly.

The two-link chain rule: if y is f of u and u is g of x, both differentiable, then the derivative is f dash evaluated at g of x, times g dash of x. Outer derivative at the inner, times inner derivative.
For three or more links, the chain just gets longer. For f of g of h of x, you peel three layers and pick up three factors, each layer contributing exactly one.
Now the workhorse patterns. A power of g: bring the exponent down, drop it by one, and multiply by g dash. This is the power rule with the chain factor attached.
Sine of g differentiates to cosine of g times g dash. And e to the g stays e to the g, but still owes the inner derivative g dash. The exponential's magic does not exempt it from the chain.
And natural log of g differentiates to g dash over g. Notice the same signature everywhere: the inner derivative g dash rides along as a multiplying factor. That factor is what students forget.

One validity note: both links must be differentiable — g at x, and f at g of x. If either link fails, at a corner or outside the domain, the rule does not apply there. Root u, for instance, breaks at u equals zero.
चलिए rule को precisely state करते हैं, फिर deeper nesting के लिए extended form, फिर वो patterns जो आप लगातार reuse करेंगे।
Two-link chain rule: अगर y, f of u है और u, g of x है, दोनों differentiable, तो derivative है f dash evaluated at g of x, times g dash of x। outer derivative inner पर, times inner derivative।
तीन या ज़्यादा links के लिए, chain बस लंबी होती है। f of g of h of x के लिए, आप तीन layers छीलते हो और तीन factors उठाते हो, हर layer exactly एक देता है।
अब workhorse patterns। g की power: exponent नीचे लाओ, एक कम करो, और g dash से multiply करो। यह power rule है chain factor के साथ।
sine of g, cosine of g times g dash में differentiate होता है। और e to the g, e to the g ही रहता है, पर inner derivative g dash का क़र्ज़दार है। exponential का जादू उसे chain से मुक्त नहीं करता।
और natural log of g, g dash over g में differentiate होता है। हर जगह वही signature देखो: inner derivative g dash multiplying factor की तरह साथ चलता है। वही factor students भूलते हैं।

एक validity note: दोनों links differentiable होने चाहिए — g at x, और f at g of x। अगर कोई link fail हो, corner पर या domain के बाहर, तो rule वहाँ apply नहीं होता। जैसे root u, u equals zero पर टूटता है।

sections.title: Chain rule: single layer and triple nesting

board_events.text: From one layer to three
Completeness check: count your factors against your layers — three layers must give three factors.

segments.text: Two examples: a clean single-layer power, then a three-layer nest where you can literally count the factors as a completeness check.
First, y equal to three x squared plus five, all to the fourth power. The outer operation is to-the-fourth, the inner is three x squared plus five.
Bring the four down, drop the power to three, keep the inner intact, then multiply by the inner derivative six x. It tidies to twenty-four x times the bracket cubed.
Now a triple nest: sine of cosine of x squared. Three layers — outer sine, middle cosine, inner x squared. Peel from the outside in.
The outer sine gives cosine of cosine of x squared. The middle cosine gives minus sine of x squared. The inner x squared gives two x. Three factors, one per layer.
Tidy it up: minus two x, times sine of x squared, times cosine of cosine of x squared. Every layer you peeled contributed exactly one factor.
That is your completeness check for any nest: count the factors against the layers. Three layers must yield three factors. A missing factor means you dropped a layer somewhere.
दो examples: एक clean single-layer power, फिर एक three-layer nest जहाँ आप factors गिन सकते हो, completeness check की तरह।
पहले, y equal to three x squared plus five, पूरा to the fourth power। outer operation है to-the-fourth, inner है three x squared plus five।
चार नीचे लाओ, power को three करो, inner को intact रखो, फिर inner derivative six x से multiply। यह twenty-four x times bracket cubed में साफ़ होता है।
अब एक triple nest: sine of cosine of x squared। तीन layers — outer sine, middle cosine, inner x squared। बाहर से अंदर छीलो।
outer sine देता है cosine of cosine of x squared। middle cosine देता है minus sine of x squared। inner x squared देता है two x। तीन factors, हर layer एक।
इसे साफ़ करो: minus two x, times sine of x squared, times cosine of cosine of x squared। हर layer जो आपने छीली, exactly एक factor दिया।
यही किसी भी nest के लिए completeness check है: factors को layers के ख़िलाफ़ गिनो। तीन layers से तीन factors आने चाहिए। कोई factor गायब मतलब कहीं एक layer छूट गई।

sections.title: The e^{3x} trap and combining chain with product

board_events.text: A signature slip, and a two-rule problem
A student writes $\frac{d}{dx}e^{3x} = e^{3x}$. What is missing?

segments.text: First the most common chain slip in one line, then a harder example where the chain rule sits inside a product.
A student differentiates e to the three x and writes e to the three x, unchanged. They treated it like plain e to the x, which is its own derivative. What did they forget?
The inside is three x, whose derivative is three. So the real answer is e to the three x times three, that is three e to the three x. The forgot-to-multiply-by-the-inside error again.
<curious>Now the harder one: y equal to x squared times root one plus x squared. This combines the product rule with the chain rule — which do we apply first?

Set v as root one plus x squared, that is one plus x squared to the half. By the chain rule, v dash is one half times the bracket to the minus half, times two x, which simplifies to x over root one plus x squared.
Now the product rule with u as x squared and v as the root. u dash v gives two x root one plus x squared, and u v dash gives x squared times x over the root. Two terms.
Put over the common denominator root one plus x squared, combine the numerator to two x plus three x cubed, and factor out an x. The clean result is x times two plus three x squared, over the root.
पहले one line में सबसे common chain slip, फिर एक harder example जहाँ chain rule एक product के अंदर बैठा है।
एक student, e to the three x differentiate करके e to the three x लिखता है, unchanged। उसने इसे plain e to the x माना, जो अपना ही derivative है। वो क्या भूला?
अंदर है three x, जिसका derivative three है। तो असली answer है e to the three x times three, यानी three e to the three x। फिर वही forgot-to-multiply-by-the-inside error।
<curious>अब harder वाला: y equal to x squared times root one plus x squared। यह product rule को chain rule के साथ combine करता है — पहले कौन सा लगाएँ?

v को root one plus x squared मानो, यानी one plus x squared to the half। chain rule से, v dash है one half times bracket to the minus half, times two x, जो simplify होता है x over root one plus x squared में।
अब product rule, u को x squared और v को root मानकर। u dash v देता है two x root one plus x squared, और u v dash देता है x squared times x over root। दो terms।
common denominator root one plus x squared पर लाओ, numerator को two x plus three x cubed में combine करो, और एक x बाहर निकालो। clean result है x times two plus three x squared, over root।

sections.subtopic: The Chain Rule — Derivatives of Composite Functions
sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: the chain rule

board_events.text: Four chain traps, and a spoken habit
Trap 1: forgetting the inner derivative — every peeled layer owes a factor.
Trap 2: differentiating the inside too early — keep it intact inside the outer derivative.
Trap 3: losing a layer in deep nesting — count factors against layers.
Trap 4: mixing chain with product — apply the product rule first, chain on the composite factor.

board_events.latex: \text{Say it: “derivative of the outside, times derivative of the inside”}

board_events.text: Mnemonic: “Outside-in, and don't forget the inside.”

segments.text: Let's bank the chain-rule mistakes and the one out-loud habit that eliminates most of them.
Trap one, forgetting the inner derivative. Writing derivative of sine of two x as cosine of two x, without the times two. Every peeled layer owes a factor — no exceptions.
Trap two, differentiating the inside too early. Keep the inner function intact sitting inside the outer derivative; only its separate derivative becomes a multiplying factor afterwards.
Trap three, losing a layer in deep nesting. For a triple composite you need exactly three factors. Count them against your layers before you declare the answer done.
Trap four, tangling chain with product. When a composite sits inside a product, apply the product rule first, then use the chain rule to differentiate the composite factor. Order keeps it clean.

The pro-tip that beats every trap: say the recipe out loud. Derivative of the outside, times derivative of the inside. For each layer you strip, immediately append its factor before doing anything else.
Carry this line out of here: outside-in, and don't forget the inside. That mechanical rhythm alone kills the dropped-inner-factor error almost entirely.
चलिए chain-rule mistakes bank करते हैं और वो एक out-loud habit जो इनमें से ज़्यादातर ख़त्म कर देती है।
Trap one, inner derivative भूलना। sine of two x का derivative cosine of two x लिखना, times two के बिना। हर peeled layer एक factor का क़र्ज़दार है — कोई exception नहीं।
Trap two, अंदर वाले को बहुत जल्दी differentiate करना। inner function को intact रखो, outer derivative के अंदर बैठा हुआ; सिर्फ उसका अलग derivative बाद में multiplying factor बनता है।
Trap three, deep nesting में एक layer खोना। triple composite के लिए exactly तीन factors चाहिए। answer done कहने से पहले उन्हें layers के ख़िलाफ़ गिनो।
Trap four, chain को product के साथ उलझाना। जब composite एक product के अंदर हो, पहले product rule लगाओ, फिर composite factor को chain rule से differentiate करो। order इसे साफ़ रखता है।
हर trap को हराने वाला pro-tip: recipe ज़ोर से बोलो। derivative of the outside, times derivative of the inside। हर layer जो आप strip करो, कुछ और करने से पहले तुरंत उसका factor जोड़ो।
यह line यहाँ से ले जाओ: outside-in, and don't forget the inside। वो mechanical rhythm अकेला dropped-inner-factor error को लगभग पूरी तरह ख़त्म कर देता है।

sections.title: When y refuses to stand alone

board_events.text: Explicit versus implicit relations
The circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=25$ tangles $y$ with $x$ — solving for $y$ splits the curve messily.
The shift: even unwritten as a formula, $y$ is secretly a function of $x$ along the curve.

board_events.caption: On the circle, slope = -x/y; it blows up to a vertical tangent where y = 0

board_events.text: Where $y = 0$ (points $(\pm 5, 0)$), the slope blows up — the formula honestly reports a vertical tangent.

segments.text: <curious>So far y has always been served up neatly as y equals some expression in x. But many curves refuse to cooperate. What then?

Take the circle x squared plus y squared equals twenty-five. Here y is tangled up with x in one equation, not isolated. You could solve for y as plus or minus a root, but that is clumsy and splits the curve into two pieces.

The core idea is a small but powerful mental shift. Even though y is not written as a formula in x, it is secretly a function of x along the curve. So treat it as a hidden function and differentiate the whole equation.

Whenever you differentiate a term containing y, the chain rule kicks in and tacks on a dy dx. So the derivative of y squared is two y times dy dx, exactly as the derivative of box squared is two box times box dash.

For the circle, differentiate both sides: two x plus two y dy dx equals zero, which rearranges to dy dx equals minus x over y. The slope depends on both x and y — normal and fine for an implicit curve.
A pure x term differentiates normally; a y term always drags along its dy dx. Collect the dy dx terms and solve algebraically. That is the entire method in one line.

One caveat: where y equals zero, at the points plus and minus five comma zero, minus x over y blows up. The derivative does not exist there, and the formula is honestly reporting a vertical tangent — not an error.
<curious>अब तक y हमेशा neatly दिया गया, y equals some expression in x। पर कई curves cooperate नहीं करते। तब क्या?

circle x squared plus y squared equals twenty-five लो। यहाँ y, x के साथ एक ही equation में उलझा है, isolated नहीं। आप y को plus या minus root के रूप में solve कर सकते हो, पर वो clumsy है और curve को दो pieces में तोड़ देता है।
Core idea एक छोटा पर powerful mental shift है। भले ही y, x में formula के रूप में नहीं लिखा, वो curve के साथ चुपके से x का function है। तो इसे hidden function मानो और पूरी equation differentiate करो।

जब भी आप y वाला term differentiate करो, chain rule आ जाता है और एक dy dx जोड़ देता है। तो y squared का derivative है two y times dy dx, बिल्कुल जैसे box squared का derivative two box times box dash होता है।

circle के लिए, दोनों sides differentiate करो: two x plus two y dy dx equals zero, जो rearrange होकर dy dx equals minus x over y बनता है। slope, x और y दोनों पर depend करती है — implicit curve के लिए normal और fine।
pure x term normally differentiate होता है; y term हमेशा अपना dy dx घसीटता है। dy dx terms इकट्ठा करो और algebraically solve करो। यही पूरा method एक line में।

एक caveat: जहाँ y equals zero, points plus और minus five comma zero पर, minus x over y blow up हो जाता है। वहाँ derivative exist नहीं करती, और formula ईमानदारी से vertical tangent report कर रहा है — कोई error नहीं।

sections.title: The governing principle and the template

board_events.text: Differentiate everything w.r.t. $x$, chain-ruling every $y$
Template step 1: differentiate term by term — chain rule on $y$-terms, product rule on mixed terms.
Template step 2: gather every $\frac{dy}{dx}$ on one side.
Second derivative: differentiate $\frac{dy}{dx}$ again, then substitute the first $\frac{dy}{dx}$ back in.

segments.text: Let's state the machinery cleanly: the governing principle, the mixed-term rule, and the step-by-step template you apply to any relation.

The governing principle: differentiate both sides with respect to x, applying the chain rule to every y term. A power of y gives n y to the n minus one, times dy dx. Any function of y gives f dash of y times dy dx.
Mixed x-y terms need the product rule too, since both factors depend on x. The derivative of x times y is one times y, plus x times dy dx — that is y plus x dy dx.
Now the general template for a relation. Step one, differentiate term by term: chain rule on the y terms, product rule on the mixed terms, ordinary differentiation on the pure x terms.
Step two, gather every dy dx term on one side of the equation and move everything else to the other side. You are setting up to factor.
Step three, factor out dy dx and divide to isolate it. The answer is generally an expression in both x and y — and that is expected, not a mistake.

For a second derivative, differentiate the first implicit derivative again with respect to x, then substitute the expression for dy dx back in, and use the original relation to simplify wherever you can.
चलिए machinery साफ़-साफ़ state करते हैं: governing principle, mixed-term rule, और step-by-step template जो आप किसी भी relation पर लगाते हो।

Governing principle: दोनों sides को x के respect में differentiate करो, हर y term पर chain rule लगाकर। y की power देती है n y to the n minus one, times dy dx। y का कोई function देता है f dash of y times dy dx।
Mixed x-y terms को product rule भी चाहिए, क्योंकि दोनों factors x पर depend करते हैं। x times y का derivative है one times y, plus x times dy dx — यानी y plus x dy dx।
अब relation के लिए general template। Step one, term by term differentiate करो: y terms पर chain rule, mixed terms पर product rule, pure x terms पर ordinary differentiation।
Step two, हर dy dx term को equation के एक side पर इकट्ठा करो और बाक़ी सब दूसरी तरफ ले जाओ। आप factor करने की तैयारी कर रहे हो।
Step three, dy dx बाहर factor करो और divide करके isolate करो। answer आम तौर पर x और y दोनों में एक expression होता है — और यह expected है, mistake नहीं।
Second derivative के लिए, पहले implicit derivative को फिर x के respect में differentiate करो, फिर dy dx की expression वापस substitute करो, और जहाँ हो सके original relation से simplify करो।

sections.title: The circle and the folium of Descartes

board_events.text: A clean warm-up and a mixed-term workout

segments.text: Two examples: the circle as a warm-up, then the folium of Descartes, where a mixed x-y term forces the product rule.
First, find dy dx for x squared plus y squared equals a squared — a general circle of radius a. The a is just a constant here.
Differentiate both sides, chain rule on y squared: two x plus two y dy dx equals zero. The constant a squared differentiates to zero. Solve, and dy dx is minus x over y.
Now the folium of Descartes: x cubed plus y cubed equals three a x y. The right side has a mixed x y term, so watch for the product rule there.
Differentiate: chain rule on y cubed gives three y squared dy dx, and the product rule on x y gives y plus x dy dx. The whole right side carries the factor three a.
Divide through by three, then gather the dy dx terms on the left and the rest on the right. Factoring dy dx, its coefficient is y squared minus a x, and the right side is a y minus x squared.
Divide to isolate it: dy dx equals a y minus x squared, over y squared minus a x. Both x and y appear, exactly as expected for an implicit curve.
दो examples: circle warm-up की तरह, फिर folium of Descartes, जहाँ एक mixed x-y term product rule पर मजबूर करता है।
पहले, x squared plus y squared equals a squared के लिए dy dx निकालो — radius a का एक general circle। यहाँ a सिर्फ एक constant है।
दोनों sides differentiate करो, y squared पर chain rule: two x plus two y dy dx equals zero। constant a squared, zero में differentiate होता है। solve करो, और dy dx है minus x over y।
अब folium of Descartes: x cubed plus y cubed equals three a x y। right side में एक mixed x y term है, तो वहाँ product rule का ध्यान रखो।
Differentiate करो: y cubed पर chain rule देता है three y squared dy dx, और x y पर product rule देता है y plus x dy dx। पूरा right side factor three a रखता है।
तीन से divide करो, फिर dy dx terms बाईं ओर और बाक़ी दाईं ओर इकट्ठा करो। dy dx factor करने पर, इसका coefficient है y squared minus a x, और right side है a y minus x squared।
isolate करने के लिए divide करो: dy dx equals a y minus x squared, over y squared minus a x। x और y दोनों आते हैं, बिल्कुल जैसा implicit curve के लिए expected।

sections.title: The dropped-factor trap and a second derivative

board_events.text: Spotting the defining error, and going to $y''$
A student differentiates $x^{2}+y^{2}=1$ and writes $2x + 2y = 0$. What went wrong?
The tell: their equation has a $y$-term but no $\frac{dy}{dx}$ — they treated $y$ as a constant.

segments.text: First the defining sin of the topic caught in the act, then a second-derivative problem with a beautiful collapse at the end.
A student differentiates x squared plus y squared equals one and writes two x plus two y equals zero. Something is badly wrong — can you name it?
The tell is that their equation has a y term but no dy dx anywhere. They differentiated y squared as if y were a constant, getting two y instead of two y dy dx. Their line is not even a derivative.
The fix restores the chain factor: two x plus two y dy dx equals zero, giving dy dx equals minus x over y. Scan your work — a y term with no dy dx means a dropped chain factor.

Now the second derivative for the unit circle. We already have the first derivative, minus x over y. Differentiate it again with respect to x, using the quotient rule and remembering d by dx of y is dy dx.

The quotient rule gives minus, the bracket y minus x times dy dx, over y squared. Substitute dy dx as minus x over y, and the numerator becomes y plus x squared over y, which tidies to y squared plus x squared over y cubed.

<excited>Now the beautiful collapse: the original relation says x squared plus y squared is one, so the whole numerator becomes one, and the second derivative reduces to a clean minus one over y cubed.
पहले topic का defining sin रंगे हाथों पकड़ा, फिर एक second-derivative problem जिसके आख़िर में एक सुंदर collapse है।
एक student, x squared plus y squared equals one differentiate करके two x plus two y equals zero लिखता है। कुछ बुरी तरह ग़लत है — आप इसका नाम बता सकते हो?
पहचान यह है कि उनकी equation में y term है पर कहीं dy dx नहीं। उन्होंने y squared को ऐसे differentiate किया जैसे y constant हो, two y dy dx की जगह two y निकाला। उनकी line derivative है ही नहीं।
Fix, chain factor बहाल करता है: two x plus two y dy dx equals zero, देता है dy dx equals minus x over y। अपना काम scan करो — बिना dy dx वाला y term मतलब एक dropped chain factor।
अब unit circle के लिए second derivative। पहला derivative हमारे पास है, minus x over y। इसे फिर x के respect में differentiate करो, quotient rule से, और याद रखो d by dx of y is dy dx।

quotient rule देता है minus, bracket y minus x times dy dx, over y squared। dy dx को minus x over y substitute करो, और numerator बनता है y plus x squared over y, जो y squared plus x squared over y cubed में साफ़ होता है।
<excited>अब सुंदर collapse: original relation कहता है x squared plus y squared एक है, तो पूरा numerator one बन जाता है, और second derivative एक clean minus one over y cubed में reduce हो जाता है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: implicit differentiation

board_events.text: Four implicit traps, and the labelling habit
Trap 1: forgetting the $\frac{dy}{dx}$ on $y$-terms — $\frac{d}{dx}(y^{2}) = 2y\frac{dy}{dx}$, never just $2y$.
Trap 2: forgetting the product rule on mixed terms — $\frac{d}{dx}(xy) = y + x\frac{dy}{dx}$.
Trap 3: trying to pre-solve for $y$ — usually unnecessary and messy.
Trap 4: second-derivative shortcuts — you must substitute the first $\frac{dy}{dx}$ back in.

board_events.latex: \text{Treat every } y \text{ as if it wore a little } (x) \text{ label: } y = y(x)

board_events.text: Mnemonic: “It's just the chain rule in disguise — every $y$ owes a $\frac{dy}{dx}$.”

segments.text: Let's bank the implicit-differentiation mistakes and the one mental label that makes the whole topic automatic.
Trap one, the defining error: forgetting the dy dx on y terms. The derivative of y squared is two y dy dx, never just two y. Drop that factor and every answer downstream is corrupted.
Trap two, forgetting the product rule on mixed terms. The derivative of x y is y plus x dy dx, not dy dx alone. Both factors depend on x, so both strips must appear.
Trap three, trying to pre-solve for y before differentiating. That is usually unnecessary and messy. Differentiate the relation as it stands and let the algebra do the work.

Trap four, second-derivative shortcuts. When finding y double dash, you must substitute the first dy dx back in, and you may use the original relation to simplify. Skipping that leaves the answer half-done.
The master pro-tip: treat every y as if it wore a little bracket x label — y is y of x. Then implicit differentiation is just the chain rule, and the dy dx factors appear automatically.
The line to remember: it is just the chain rule in disguise — every y owes a dy dx. And final answers naturally involve both x and y; that is expected, not a mistake.
चलिए implicit-differentiation mistakes bank करते हैं और वो एक mental label जो पूरे topic को automatic बना देता है।
Trap one, defining error: y terms पर dy dx भूलना। y squared का derivative है two y dy dx, कभी सिर्फ two y नहीं। वो factor drop करो और आगे का हर answer corrupt हो जाता है।
Trap two, mixed terms पर product rule भूलना। x y का derivative है y plus x dy dx, अकेला dy dx नहीं। दोनों factors x पर depend करते हैं, तो दोनों strips आने चाहिए।
Trap three, differentiate करने से पहले y के लिए pre-solve करने की कोशिश। वो आम तौर पर unnecessary और messy है। relation को जैसा है वैसा differentiate करो और algebra को काम करने दो।

Trap four, second-derivative shortcuts। y double dash निकालते समय, आपको पहला dy dx वापस substitute करना ही है, और simplify करने के लिए original relation use कर सकते हो। इसे skip करना answer आधा-अधूरा छोड़ देता है।
Master pro-tip: हर y को ऐसे treat करो जैसे उस पर एक छोटा bracket x label लगा हो — y is y of x। फिर implicit differentiation सिर्फ chain rule है, और dy dx factors अपने आप आ जाते हैं।
याद रखने वाली line: यह सिर्फ chain rule का भेस है — हर y एक dy dx का क़र्ज़दार है। और final answers स्वाभाविक रूप से x और y दोनों रखते हैं; यह expected है, mistake नहीं।

sections.title: Inverse trig and the double-angle disguise

board_events.text: “Which angle gives this ratio?”
If $y = \sin^{-1}x$ then $\sin y = x$; differentiate implicitly and solve for $\frac{dy}{dx}$.
The real exam drama: monstrous-looking expressions that hide a double-angle formula.
