board_events.text: Trap: $\tan^{-1}(\tan 2\theta) = 2\theta$ only when $2\theta$ lies in $(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2})$ — the simplification is piecewise.

segments.text: <curious>An inverse trig function answers a simple question: which angle gives this ratio? Inverse sine of x is the angle whose sine is x. Differentiating them needs no new magic.

If y is inverse sine of x, then sine y equals x. Differentiate both sides implicitly, which you just learned, and solve for dy dx. Out pops one over root one minus x squared. Every inverse-trig derivative is born this way.
But the real exam drama lies elsewhere. Examiners adore expressions like inverse tan of two x over one minus x squared, which look monstrous to differentiate head-on. The secret is to simplify first.
These are double-angle formulas in disguise. Let x equal tan theta. Then two x over one minus x squared becomes two tan theta over one minus tan squared theta, which is exactly tan of two theta.

The substitution triangle helps you see it: with x equals tan theta, the opposite side is x, the adjacent is one, and the hypotenuse is root one plus x squared. Every trig ratio of theta reads straight off this triangle.
So the monster equals inverse tan of tan two theta, which is two theta, which is two inverse tan of x. Differentiating that is a one-liner: two over one plus x squared. The brutal problem melts away.

<whisper>But read the fine print. The cancellation is only valid when two theta stays in the principal range of inverse tan. Outside it, the identity differs by a constant on each piece — so these simplifications are piecewise, and you must state the range.

<curious>एक inverse trig function एक simple सवाल का जवाब देता है: कौन सा angle यह ratio देता है? inverse sine of x वो angle है जिसका sine x है। इन्हें differentiate करने के लिए कोई नया जादू नहीं चाहिए।

अगर y, inverse sine of x है, तो sine y equals x। दोनों sides implicitly differentiate करो, जो आपने अभी सीखा, और dy dx के लिए solve करो। निकलता है one over root one minus x squared। हर inverse-trig derivative इसी तरह पैदा होता है।

पर असली exam drama कहीं और है। examiners को inverse tan of two x over one minus x squared जैसी expressions बहुत पसंद हैं, जो सीधे differentiate करने में monstrous लगती हैं। secret है पहले simplify करना।
ये double-angle formulas का भेस हैं। x को tan theta मानो। तो two x over one minus x squared बनता है two tan theta over one minus tan squared theta, जो exactly tan of two theta है।

Substitution triangle इसे देखने में मदद करता है: x equals tan theta के साथ, opposite side x है, adjacent one है, और hypotenuse root one plus x squared। theta का हर trig ratio सीधे इस triangle से पढ़ा जाता है।
तो monster equals inverse tan of tan two theta, जो two theta है, जो two inverse tan of x है। उसे differentiate करना one-liner है: two over one plus x squared। brutal problem पिघल जाता है।

<whisper>पर fine print पढ़ो। cancellation सिर्फ तब valid है जब two theta, inverse tan के principal range में रहे। इसके बाहर, identity हर piece पर एक constant से अलग होती है — तो ये simplifications piecewise हैं, और आपको range बताना ही होगा।

sections.title: The six derivatives and the golden identities

board_events.text: The standard results and the substitution keys
Substitution keys: $\frac{2x}{1-x^{2}}, \frac{1-x^{2}}{1+x^{2}} \Rightarrow x = \tan\theta$; $2x\sqrt{1-x^{2}} \Rightarrow x = \sin\theta$; $\sqrt{x^{2}-1} \Rightarrow x = \sec\theta$.

segments.text: Let's collect the six standard inverse-trig derivatives, then the golden substitution identities that unlock the hard problems.
Inverse sine gives one over root one minus x squared. Inverse cosine is the same magnitude with a minus sign. Both live on magnitude of x below one.
Inverse tan gives one over one plus x squared, valid for all real x. Inverse cotangent is again the same magnitude with a minus sign in front.
Inverse secant gives one over the absolute value of x, times root x squared minus one. Inverse cosecant carries the minus. That absolute value is essential, and both need magnitude of x above one.

Now the golden identities. Two inverse tan of x equals all three of these disguised forms: inverse tan of two x over one minus x squared, inverse sine of two x over one plus x squared, and inverse cosine of one minus x squared over one plus x squared.

Two more: two inverse sine of x equals inverse sine of two x root one minus x squared, and three inverse sine of x equals inverse sine of three x minus four x cubed. These are the double and triple angle sine formulas, read backwards.

And the substitution keys to memorise: the two x over one minus x squared and one minus x squared over one plus x squared forms scream x equals tan theta; two x root one minus x squared screams x equals sine theta; and root x squared minus one screams x equals secant theta.
चलिए छह standard inverse-trig derivatives collect करते हैं, फिर वो golden substitution identities जो hard problems unlock करती हैं।
Inverse sine देता है one over root one minus x squared। inverse cosine वही magnitude है minus sign के साथ। दोनों magnitude of x, one से नीचे रहते हैं।
Inverse tan देता है one over one plus x squared, सब real x के लिए valid। inverse cotangent फिर वही magnitude है, आगे minus sign के साथ।
Inverse secant देता है one over absolute value of x, times root x squared minus one। inverse cosecant minus रखता है। वो absolute value essential है, और दोनों को magnitude of x, one से ऊपर चाहिए।

अब golden identities। two inverse tan of x, इन तीनों disguised forms के बराबर है: inverse tan of two x over one minus x squared, inverse sine of two x over one plus x squared, और inverse cosine of one minus x squared over one plus x squared।

दो और: two inverse sine of x equals inverse sine of two x root one minus x squared, और three inverse sine of x equals inverse sine of three x minus four x cubed। ये double और triple angle sine formulas हैं, उल्टा पढ़े हुए।

और याद रखने वाली substitution keys: two x over one minus x squared और one minus x squared over one plus x squared forms चिल्लाती हैं x equals tan theta; two x root one minus x squared चिल्लाता है x equals sine theta; और root x squared minus one चिल्लाता है x equals secant theta।

sections.title: Deriving the results, and a first application

board_events.text: Where two derivatives come from, plus a chain-rule warm-up

segments.text: Let's derive two of the standard results from implicit differentiation, then apply the plain chain rule to a simple inverse-tan.
Let y be inverse tan of x, so tan y equals x. Differentiate both sides: the chain rule on tan y gives secant squared y times dy dx, and that equals one.
So dy dx is one over secant squared y. Use the identity secant squared equals one plus tan squared, and tan y is x, so it becomes one over one plus x squared. Clean and derived, not memorised.
Similarly, let y be inverse sine of x, so sine y equals x. Differentiating gives cosine y times dy dx equals one, so dy dx is one over cosine y.
Write cosine y as root one minus sine squared y, taking the positive root because cosine is non-negative on the principal range. Since sine y is x, this is one over root one minus x squared.
Now a Board-level warm-up: differentiate inverse tan of two x. This is just the chain rule — outer derivative one over one plus the inside squared, times the inner derivative two.
The inside two x squares to four x squared, and the factor two rides on top, giving two over one plus four x squared. No substitution needed here — it is a genuine composite, not a disguise.
चलिए दो standard results implicit differentiation से derive करते हैं, फिर एक simple inverse-tan पर plain chain rule लगाते हैं।
y को inverse tan of x मानो, तो tan y equals x। दोनों sides differentiate करो: tan y पर chain rule देता है secant squared y times dy dx, और वो equals one।
तो dy dx है one over secant squared y। identity use करो secant squared equals one plus tan squared, और tan y, x है, तो यह बनता है one over one plus x squared। clean और derived, रटा नहीं।
इसी तरह, y को inverse sine of x मानो, तो sine y equals x। differentiate करने पर cosine y times dy dx equals one, तो dy dx है one over cosine y।
cosine y को root one minus sine squared y लिखो, positive root लेते हुए क्योंकि principal range पर cosine non-negative है। चूँकि sine y, x है, यह one over root one minus x squared है।
अब एक Board-level warm-up: inverse tan of two x differentiate करो। यह सिर्फ chain rule है — outer derivative one over one plus inside squared, times inner derivative two।
अंदर two x, four x squared में square होता है, और factor two ऊपर बैठता है, देता है two over one plus four x squared। यहाँ कोई substitution नहीं चाहिए — यह असली composite है, भेस नहीं।

sections.title: Substitution power and the piecewise-sign trap

board_events.text: A monster that melts, and one that flips sign
For $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\lt x\le 1$: $y = \pi - 2\sin^{-1}x$, so $y' = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$ — opposite sign!
Lesson: a single formula for all $x$ is wrong on half the domain — always check the principal range.

segments.text: Two substitution examples. The first melts cleanly. The second hides a trap so sharp it flips the sign of your derivative on half the domain.
First, differentiate inverse tan of two x over one minus x squared, on the interval minus one to one. Head-on this is painful, so substitute x equals tan theta.

The inside becomes tan of two theta. On this range two theta stays inside the principal interval, so the cancellation is valid: y is two theta, that is two inverse tan of x, and the derivative is two over one plus x squared.

Now the trap. Differentiate inverse sine of two x root one minus x squared. Substitute x equals sine theta, so two x root one minus x squared becomes two sine theta cosine theta, which is sine of two theta.
For magnitude of x up to one over root two, two theta stays in the principal range of inverse sine, so y is two inverse sine of x, and the derivative is two over root one minus x squared.

<whisper>But for x above one over root two, two theta leaves the principal range, and the identity becomes pi minus two inverse sine of x. Now the derivative is minus two over root one minus x squared — the opposite sign.

The lesson is sharp: a student who writes one formula for all x is wrong on half the domain. With inverse-trig substitutions, always check whether the multiple angle stays inside the principal range — the sign itself is piecewise.
दो substitution examples। पहला cleanly पिघलता है। दूसरा इतना sharp trap छिपाता है कि आधे domain पर आपके derivative का sign flip कर देता है।
पहले, inverse tan of two x over one minus x squared differentiate करो, interval minus one to one पर। सीधे यह painful है, तो x equals tan theta substitute करो।

अंदर बनता है tan of two theta। इस range पर two theta principal interval के अंदर रहता है, तो cancellation valid है: y is two theta, यानी two inverse tan of x, और derivative two over one plus x squared।

अब trap। inverse sine of two x root one minus x squared differentiate करो। x equals sine theta substitute करो, तो two x root one minus x squared बनता है two sine theta cosine theta, जो sine of two theta है।
magnitude of x, one over root two तक के लिए, two theta inverse sine के principal range में रहता है, तो y is two inverse sine of x, और derivative two over root one minus x squared।

<whisper>पर x, one over root two से ऊपर के लिए, two theta principal range छोड़ देता है, और identity बनती है pi minus two inverse sine of x। अब derivative है minus two over root one minus x squared — उल्टा sign।

Lesson sharp है: जो student सब x के लिए एक formula लिखता है, वो आधे domain पर ग़लत है। inverse-trig substitutions के साथ, हमेशा check करो कि multiple angle principal range के अंदर रहता है या नहीं — sign ख़ुद piecewise है।

sections.title: A fearsome expression reduced to a clean half

board_events.text: Half-angle magic on an intimidating fraction
The whole game: recognise the disguise, substitute, collapse, then differentiate the simple result.

segments.text: <excited>An Advanced-level gem: an expression that looks genuinely intimidating collapses, through a half-angle identity, to a clean one half.

Differentiate inverse tan of the fraction root one plus x squared minus one, over x. Head-on this is a nightmare, so substitute x equals tan theta, which makes root one plus x squared equal secant theta.
The fraction becomes secant theta minus one over tan theta. Rewrite in sines and cosines, and it tidies to one minus cosine theta, over sine theta.

Now the half-angle identities: one minus cosine theta is two sine squared theta over two, and sine theta is two sine theta over two cosine theta over two. The twos and one sine cancel, leaving tan of theta over two.
So y is inverse tan of tan theta over two, which cancels to theta over two, which is one half inverse tan of x. The monster has become a clean multiple of a standard inverse tan.

Differentiating is now trivial: one half times one over one plus x squared, that is one over two times one plus x squared. A genuinely intimidating expression reduced to a clean half — the payoff of the substitution method.
That is the whole game of this subtopic: recognise the disguise, substitute the matching trig form, collapse the inner expression, and only then differentiate the simple result you are left with.
<excited>एक Advanced-level gem: एक expression जो सच में intimidating लगती है, half-angle identity से एक clean one half में collapse हो जाती है।

inverse tan of fraction root one plus x squared minus one, over x differentiate करो। सीधे यह nightmare है, तो x equals tan theta substitute करो, जो root one plus x squared को secant theta बना देता है।
fraction बनता है secant theta minus one over tan theta। sines और cosines में rewrite करो, और यह one minus cosine theta, over sine theta में साफ़ होता है।

अब half-angle identities: one minus cosine theta है two sine squared theta over two, और sine theta है two sine theta over two cosine theta over two। twos और एक sine cancel, बचता है tan of theta over two।
तो y है inverse tan of tan theta over two, जो theta over two में cancel होता है, जो one half inverse tan of x है। monster एक standard inverse tan का clean multiple बन गया।

अब differentiate करना trivial है: one half times one over one plus x squared, यानी one over two times one plus x squared। एक सच में intimidating expression एक clean half में reduce — substitution method का payoff।
यही इस subtopic का पूरा खेल है: भेस पहचानो, matching trig form substitute करो, inner expression collapse करो, और तभी उस simple result को differentiate करो जो बचा है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: inverse-trig derivatives

board_events.text: Four inverse-trig traps, and a pattern-spotting eye
Trap 1: ignoring principal-range domains — the identities, and sometimes the derivative's sign, are piecewise.
Trap 2: table sign mix-ups — $\cos^{-1}, \cot^{-1}, \csc^{-1}$ carry the minus.
Trap 3: dropping $|x|$ in $\sec^{-1}$ and $\csc^{-1}$ — it matters for $x\lt -1$.
Trap 4: brute-forcing instead of substituting — grinding the quotient rule invites algebra errors.
Mnemonic: “Substitute, collapse the double angle, then differentiate — and mind the range.”

segments.text: Let's bank the inverse-trig mistakes and the pattern recognition that turns a five-minute grind into a thirty-second answer.

Trap one, ignoring principal-range domains. Writing one simplified formula for all x. These identities, and sometimes even the sign of the derivative, are piecewise. Always check where the multiple angle stays in range.
Trap two, table sign mix-ups. The cofunctions — inverse cosine, inverse cotangent, inverse cosecant — carry minus signs. Pairing them wrongly with inverse sine, tan, or secant is a common slip.
Trap three, dropping the absolute value in inverse secant and inverse cosecant. That absolute value of x genuinely matters for x below minus one; without it your derivative has the wrong sign there.
Trap four, brute-forcing instead of substituting. Grinding the quotient or chain rule on two x over one minus x squared wastes time and invites algebra errors. Substitution is far safer and faster.
The pro-tip: train your eye to spot the disguises. Two x over one minus x squared screams tan theta; two x root one minus x squared screams sine theta; root x squared minus one screams secant theta.
The mnemonic to carry out: substitute, collapse the double angle, then differentiate — and mind the range. Recognising the pattern is the whole win here, but always finish by stating the valid range.
चलिए inverse-trig mistakes bank करते हैं और वो pattern recognition जो पाँच-मिनट की पिसाई को तीस-सेकंड के answer में बदल देती है।

Trap one, principal-range domains ignore करना। सब x के लिए एक simplified formula लिखना। ये identities, और कभी-कभी derivative का sign भी, piecewise हैं। हमेशा check करो कि multiple angle कहाँ range में रहता है।
Trap two, table sign mix-ups। cofunctions — inverse cosine, inverse cotangent, inverse cosecant — minus signs रखते हैं। इन्हें inverse sine, tan, या secant के साथ ग़लत pair करना common slip है।
Trap three, inverse secant और inverse cosecant में absolute value drop करना। वो absolute value of x, x के minus one से नीचे सच में matter करता है; इसके बिना वहाँ आपके derivative का sign ग़लत होता है।

Trap four, substitute करने की जगह brute-force करना। two x over one minus x squared पर quotient या chain rule पीसना time waste करता है और algebra errors बुलाता है। substitution कहीं safer और faster है।

Pro-tip: अपनी आँख को भेस पहचानने के लिए train करो। two x over one minus x squared चिल्लाता है tan theta; two x root one minus x squared चिल्लाता है sine theta; root x squared minus one चिल्लाता है secant theta।
साथ ले जाने वाला mnemonic: substitute, collapse the double angle, then differentiate — and mind the range। pattern पहचानना ही यहाँ पूरी जीत है, पर हमेशा valid range बताकर ख़त्म करो।

sections.title: The logarithm rides in as a rescuer

board_events.text: Three functions, one that breaks both rules
$x^{5}$: power rule (constant exponent). $5^{x}$: exponential rule (constant base).
$x^{x}$: variable base AND variable exponent — neither rule applies. We are stuck.
The log is a currency converter: it turns multiplication and powers into addition.
It also tames long products: $\ln$ shatters a product into a clean sum of logs.
Take the log, then differentiate — that single trick is logarithmic differentiation.

segments.text: <curious>Differentiate three functions: x to the five, then five to the x, then x to the x. The first two are routine. The third breaks everything. Why?

x to the five is a piece of cake — the power rule handles a constant exponent, giving five x to the fourth. Five to the x is also routine — the exponential rule handles a constant base, giving five to the x times natural log of five.

But x to the x has a variable in both the base and the exponent at once. The power rule assumes the exponent stands still; the exponential rule assumes the base stands still. Here nothing stands still, so we are stuck.
This is where the logarithm rides in. Think of it as a currency converter in a busy market: it turns the hard currency of multiplication and powers into the easy currency of addition.
Take natural log of both sides of y equals x to the x. The troublesome exponent slides down to become an ordinary factor: log y equals x times log x, which we can actually differentiate.
It earns its keep a second way too: when y is a long, ugly product or quotient of many factors, log shatters that product into a clean sum of logs, and a sum is trivial to differentiate term by term.
That single trick — take the log, then differentiate — is logarithmic differentiation. One condition to remember: the base must be positive, since the log of a non-positive number is undefined.
<curious>तीन functions differentiate करो: x to the five, फिर five to the x, फिर x to the x। पहले दो routine हैं। तीसरा सब कुछ तोड़ देता है। क्यों?

x to the five आसान है — power rule constant exponent संभालता है, देता है five x to the fourth। five to the x भी routine है — exponential rule constant base संभालता है, देता है five to the x times natural log of five।
पर x to the x में base और exponent दोनों में एक साथ variable है। power rule मानता है exponent स्थिर है; exponential rule मानता है base स्थिर है। यहाँ कुछ भी स्थिर नहीं, तो हम फँस गए।
यहीं logarithm आता है। इसे एक busy market का currency converter समझो: यह multiplication और powers की hard currency को addition की easy currency में बदल देता है।
y equals x to the x के दोनों sides का natural log लो। troublesome exponent नीचे खिसककर एक ordinary factor बन जाता है: log y equals x times log x, जिसे हम सच में differentiate कर सकते हैं।

यह दूसरे तरीक़े से भी अपनी क़ीमत वसूल करता है: जब y कई factors का लंबा, बदसूरत product या quotient हो, log उस product को logs के clean sum में तोड़ देता है, और sum को term by term differentiate करना trivial है।
वो एक trick — log लो, फिर differentiate करो — ही logarithmic differentiation है। याद रखने की एक शर्त: base positive होना चाहिए, क्योंकि non-positive number का log undefined है।

sections.title: Parametric differentiation: the puppeteer

board_events.text: When $x$ and $y$ are both driven by a third variable
A cricket ball: time drives both height $y$ and horizontal distance $x$.
Time is the puppeteer; $x$ and $y$ are two puppets on its strings.
A Ferris wheel: your seat is $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, driven by angle $\theta$.
Validity: the slope needs $dx/dt \neq 0$.
The differentiation just compares the puppets' motions — rates, then their ratio.

segments.text: Now the second idea. Sometimes x and y are not tied to each other directly; instead, both are controlled by a third, behind-the-scenes variable — a parameter, usually t for time or theta for angle.

Picture a cricket ball flying through the air. You do not naturally describe its height as a function of its horizontal distance. What you know is how time drives both — x from the horizontal speed, y from speed minus the pull of gravity.
Time is the puppeteer; x and y are the two puppets dangling from its strings. To get the slope of the ball's path, you ask how fast each puppet responds to the puppeteer and take the ratio.
So dy dx equals the rate of y with respect to t, divided by the rate of x with respect to t. Each is an ordinary derivative in the parameter; the ratio gives the slope in the x-y plane.
Or picture a giant wheel at a village fair: your seat's position is most naturally given by the rotation angle, x equals r cosine theta and y equals r sine theta. The angle is the puppet-master here.
One validity guard: the slope needs the rate of x with respect to t to be non-zero. Where that rate is zero, the slope blows up — a vertical tangent — and the formula breaks.

That is the whole intuition: with a parameter pulling the strings, differentiation just compares the puppets' motions — find each rate, then take their ratio. The second derivative, as we will see, needs one extra turn of the crank.
अब दूसरा idea। कभी-कभी x और y सीधे एक-दूसरे से बंधे नहीं होते; बल्कि दोनों एक तीसरे, पर्दे के पीछे वाले variable से control होते हैं — एक parameter, आम तौर पर t time के लिए या theta angle के लिए।

Socho एक cricket ball हवा में उड़ती हुई। आप स्वाभाविक रूप से उसकी height को horizontal distance के function के रूप में नहीं बताते। आप जानते हो कि time दोनों को कैसे चलाता है — x horizontal speed से, y speed minus gravity की खिंचाई से।
Time puppeteer है; x और y उसकी डोरियों पर लटके दो puppets हैं। ball के path की slope पाने के लिए, आप पूछते हो हर puppet puppeteer पर कितनी तेज़ी से react करता है और ratio ले लेते हो।
तो dy dx equals rate of y with respect to t, divided by rate of x with respect to t। हर एक parameter में ordinary derivative है; ratio, x-y plane में slope देता है।
या socho एक गाँव के मेले का giant wheel: आपकी seat की position सबसे स्वाभाविक रूप से rotation angle से मिलती है, x equals r cosine theta और y equals r sine theta। यहाँ angle puppet-master है।
एक validity guard: slope को rate of x with respect to t का non-zero होना चाहिए। जहाँ वो rate zero है, slope blow up कर जाती है — vertical tangent — और formula टूट जाता है।

यही पूरी intuition है: एक parameter डोरियाँ खींचते हुए, differentiation बस puppets की motions compare करता है — हर rate निकालो, फिर उनका ratio लो। second derivative, जैसा हम देखेंगे, crank का एक extra घुमाव माँगता है।

sections.title: The engines: master u^v formula and parametric derivatives

board_events.text: The formulas that do the heavy lifting

board_events.latex: \ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b, \quad \ln\tfrac{a}{b} = \ln a - \ln b, \quad \ln(a^{n}) = n\ln a

board_events.text: It is NOT $\dfrac{d^{2}y/dt^{2}}{d^{2}x/dt^{2}}$ — you cannot cancel the $dt$'s like numbers.

segments.text: Let's state the engines: the logarithmic-differentiation relation, the master formula for a variable-power function, and the two parametric derivatives — with a sharp warning on the second.
The engine of log differentiation: the derivative of log y is one over y, times dy dx. Never forget that one-over-y — it is the chain rule on log y, and dropping it silently corrupts every answer.

The master formula for u to the v: it is the sum of two pieces. The exponential-rule piece, with the base frozen, is u to the v times log u times v dash. The power-rule piece, with the exponent frozen, is v times u to the v minus one times u dash.
The log properties you use to simplify before differentiating: log of a product is a sum of logs, log of a quotient is a difference, and log of a power brings the exponent down to the front.
The parametric first derivative: with x and y both functions of t, dy dx is the rate of y over the rate of x, both taken in t. Valid wherever the rate of x is non-zero.
The parametric second derivative: differentiate the already-found slope with respect to t, then divide by the rate of x once more. This comes from applying the chain-rule operator a second time.

And the sharp warning: the second derivative is not the ratio of the two second t-derivatives. You cannot cancel the d-t's like numbers. Slope first, differentiate by t, divide by the rate of x one more time.
चलिए engines state करते हैं: logarithmic-differentiation relation, variable-power function का master formula, और दो parametric derivatives — दूसरे पर एक तीखी warning के साथ।
log differentiation का engine: log y का derivative है one over y, times dy dx। उस one-over-y को कभी मत भूलो — यह log y पर chain rule है, और इसे drop करना चुपचाप हर answer corrupt कर देता है।

u to the v का master formula: यह दो pieces का sum है। exponential-rule piece, base frozen के साथ, है u to the v times log u times v dash। power-rule piece, exponent frozen के साथ, है v times u to the v minus one times u dash।
differentiate करने से पहले simplify करने के लिए log properties: product का log, logs का sum है, quotient का log एक difference है, और power का log exponent को आगे नीचे ले आता है।
parametric first derivative: x और y दोनों t के functions होने पर, dy dx है rate of y over rate of x, दोनों t में लिए हुए। जहाँ rate of x non-zero है, वहाँ valid।
parametric second derivative: पहले से मिली slope को t के respect में differentiate करो, फिर rate of x से एक बार और divide करो। यह chain-rule operator को दूसरी बार लगाने से आता है।
और तीखी warning: second derivative, दो second t-derivatives का ratio नहीं है। आप d-t को numbers की तरह cancel नहीं कर सकते। पहले slope, फिर t से differentiate, फिर rate of x से एक बार और divide।

sections.title: Deriving the master formula, and x^{sin x}

board_events.text: Where $u^{v}$ comes from, and a Board application

board_events.latex: y = x^{\sin x}, \; x\gt 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \ln y = \sin x\ln x

segments.text: Let's derive the master formula so you trust it, then apply logarithmic differentiation to the classic x to the sine x.
Start with y equals f of x to the g of x, with f positive so the log is defined. Take the natural log of both sides; the exponent g slides down to the front, giving log y equals g times log f.
Differentiate both sides. The left uses the chain rule on log y, giving one over y times dy dx. The right uses the product rule on g times log f, giving g dash log f plus g times f dash over f.
Multiply through by y and substitute y back as f to the g. That is the master formula: the whole original function, times the bracket combining the exponential piece and the power piece.
Now the application. For y equals x to the sine x, take logs: log y equals sine x times log x. Both the exponent and base are variable, so this genuinely needs the log trick.
Differentiate: the left gives one over y times dy dx. The right, by the product rule, gives cosine x times log x, plus sine x times one over x.
Multiply by y and substitute back: the derivative is x to the sine x, times the bracket cosine x log x plus sine x over x. Notice how the master formula and the take-logs method agree perfectly.
चलिए master formula derive करते हैं ताकि आप भरोसा करो, फिर classic x to the sine x पर logarithmic differentiation लगाते हैं।
y equals f of x to the g of x से शुरू करो, f positive ताकि log defined हो। दोनों sides का natural log लो; exponent g आगे नीचे खिसकता है, देता है log y equals g times log f।

दोनों sides differentiate करो। left, log y पर chain rule use करता है, देता है one over y times dy dx। right, g times log f पर product rule use करता है, देता है g dash log f plus g times f dash over f।
y से multiply करो और y को f to the g वापस substitute करो। यही master formula है: पूरा original function, times वो bracket जो exponential piece और power piece को जोड़ता है।
अब application। y equals x to the sine x के लिए, logs लो: log y equals sine x times log x। exponent और base दोनों variable हैं, तो इसे सच में log trick चाहिए।
Differentiate करो: left देता है one over y times dy dx। right, product rule से, देता है cosine x times log x, plus sine x times one over x।
y से multiply करो और वापस substitute करो: derivative है x to the sine x, times bracket cosine x log x plus sine x over x। ध्यान दो master formula और take-logs method कैसे perfectly agree करते हैं।

sections.title: The astroid, and the parametric second-derivative trap

board_events.text: A clean parametric slope, then the most-tested slip
The trap: writing $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = \frac{d^{2}y/dt^{2}}{d^{2}x/dt^{2}} = \frac{0}{2a} = 0$ — wrong.

segments.text: Two parametric examples: the astroid, where everything cancels beautifully, then the second-derivative trap that examiners set again and again.
First the astroid, x equals a cosine cubed t and y equals a sine cubed t. Differentiate each with respect to t, using the chain rule on the cubes.
The rate of x is minus three a cosine squared t sine t, and the rate of y is three a sine squared t cosine t. Now take the ratio for the slope.

The three a's cancel, and one power each of sine and cosine cancels, leaving minus sine t over cosine t, that is minus tan t. That clean cancellation is the hallmark of a well-posed parametric problem.
Now the trap. For x equals a t squared and y equals two a t, the rate of y is two a and the rate of x is two a t, so the slope dy dx is one over t. So far, so easy.

<whisper>Here is the most-tested error: cancelling the d-t's and writing the second derivative as zero over two a, which is zero. That is simply wrong — it would falsely claim the parabola has zero curvature everywhere.

The correct route: differentiate the slope one over t with respect to t, giving minus one over t squared, then divide by the rate of x, two a t. The real answer is minus one over two a t cubed. Chant: slope, differentiate by t, divide by the rate of x.
दो parametric examples: astroid, जहाँ सब कुछ खूबसूरती से cancel होता है, फिर वो second-derivative trap जो examiners बार-बार लगाते हैं।
पहले astroid, x equals a cosine cubed t और y equals a sine cubed t। हर एक को t के respect में differentiate करो, cubes पर chain rule से।
rate of x है minus three a cosine squared t sine t, और rate of y है three a sine squared t cosine t। अब slope के लिए ratio लो।
तीन a cancel होते हैं, और sine और cosine की एक-एक power cancel होती है, बचता है minus sine t over cosine t, यानी minus tan t। वो clean cancellation एक well-posed parametric problem की पहचान है।
अब trap। x equals a t squared और y equals two a t के लिए, rate of y है two a और rate of x है two a t, तो slope dy dx है one over t। अब तक आसान।
<whisper>यहाँ सबसे ज़्यादा test होने वाला error: d-t को cancel करके second derivative को zero over two a लिखना, जो zero है। यह बस ग़लत है — यह झूठा दावा करेगा कि parabola की हर जगह zero curvature है।

सही रास्ता: slope one over t को t के respect में differentiate करो, देता है minus one over t squared, फिर rate of x, two a t से divide करो। असली answer है minus one over two a t cubed। बोलो: slope, t से differentiate, rate of x से divide।

sections.title: An Advanced proof: x = sin t, y = sin pt

board_events.text: Proving a differential-equation relation

board_events.latex: x y' = \frac{p\sin t\cos pt}{\cos t}, \qquad p^{2}y = p^{2}\sin pt

board_events.text: Add all three: the $\frac{p\sin t\cos pt}{\cos t}$ terms cancel and the $\pm p^{2}\sin pt$ pair cancels $\Rightarrow 0$.

segments.text: <excited>An Advanced-level classic: given x equals sine t and y equals sine p t, prove a clean differential-equation relation. Watch the awkward terms annihilate at the end.
The target relation is one minus x squared times y double dash, minus x times y dash, plus p squared y, equals zero. We build up dy dx and y double dash parametrically.
The rate of x is cosine t, the rate of y is p cosine p t. So the first derivative, y dash, is p cosine p t over cosine t. Keep this handy.

For y double dash, differentiate that slope with respect to t by the quotient rule, then divide by cosine t once more. It comes out as minus p squared sine p t cosine t, plus p sine t cosine p t, all over cosine cubed t.

Now assemble, using one minus x squared equals one minus sine squared t equals cosine squared t. Multiplying y double dash by cosine squared t cancels two powers of cosine, leaving minus p squared sine p t, plus p sine t cosine p t over cosine t.
The middle term, x times y dash, is sine t times p cosine p t over cosine t, that is p sine t cosine p t over cosine t. And p squared y is simply p squared sine p t.

Add the three pieces. The two p sine t cosine p t over cosine t terms cancel each other, and the plus and minus p squared sine p t pair cancels too. Everything annihilates to zero — the relation holds identically. Proof done.
<excited>एक Advanced-level classic: x equals sine t और y equals sine p t दिए हैं, एक clean differential-equation relation prove करो। आख़िर में awkward terms को नष्ट होते देखो।
Target relation है one minus x squared times y double dash, minus x times y dash, plus p squared y, equals zero। हम dy dx और y double dash को parametrically बनाते हैं।
rate of x है cosine t, rate of y है p cosine p t। तो first derivative, y dash, है p cosine p t over cosine t। इसे संभालकर रखो।

y double dash के लिए, उस slope को t के respect में quotient rule से differentiate करो, फिर cosine t से एक बार और divide करो। यह निकलता है minus p squared sine p t cosine t, plus p sine t cosine p t, सब cosine cubed t के ऊपर।

अब assemble करो, one minus x squared equals one minus sine squared t equals cosine squared t use करते हुए। y double dash को cosine squared t से multiply करने पर cosine की दो powers cancel होती हैं, बचता है minus p squared sine p t, plus p sine t cosine p t over cosine t।
middle term, x times y dash, है sine t times p cosine p t over cosine t, यानी p sine t cosine p t over cosine t। और p squared y बस p squared sine p t है।

तीनों pieces जोड़ो। दो p sine t cosine p t over cosine t terms एक-दूसरे को cancel करते हैं, और plus और minus p squared sine p t की जोड़ी भी cancel होती है। सब कुछ zero में नष्ट — relation identically holds। Proof done।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: log & parametric

board_events.text: Four traps, and two direct-write shortcuts
Trap 1: dropping the $\frac{1}{y}$ — $\frac{d}{dx}\ln y = \frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx}$, not $\frac{1}{y}$.
Trap 2: the half-rule on $u^{v}$ — writing only $u^{v}\ln u$ or only $v\,u^{v-1}$. You need their sum.
Trap 3: the parametric second-derivative ratio — always slope first, differentiate by $t$, divide by $dx/dt$.
Trap 4: ignoring the positive-base condition — use $|\cdot|$ or state the domain when the base can be $\le 0$.
For parametric curves, simplify $\frac{dy}{dx}$ fully before substituting a value — the constants almost always cancel.

segments.text: Let's bank the log and parametric mistakes, plus two shortcuts that let you write answers directly under time pressure.
Trap one, dropping the one over y. The derivative of log y is one over y times dy dx, not just one over y. The y is a function of x, so the chain rule demands that extra dy dx.

Trap two, the half-rule on u to the v. Writing only the exponential piece, or only the power piece. Both are halves of the truth; the real answer is their sum. A one-piece answer to u to the v is always incomplete.

Trap three, the parametric second-derivative ratio. Never use the ratio of the two second t-derivatives. Always: find the slope, differentiate it with respect to t, then divide by the rate of x once more.
Trap four, ignoring the positive-base condition. Log differentiation needs a positive base; if the base can be zero or negative, work with absolute values or restrict the domain, and say so.
The first pro-tip: for any u to the v, skip re-deriving and write the answer directly as the exponential piece plus the power piece. That single line covers every variable-power question.

The second pro-tip: for parametric curves, fully simplify dy dx before plugging in any value. The constants almost always cancel, and a clean symbolic slope is far less error-prone to substitute into.
चलिए log और parametric mistakes bank करते हैं, साथ में दो shortcuts जो time pressure में answers सीधे लिखने देते हैं।
Trap one, one over y drop करना। log y का derivative है one over y times dy dx, सिर्फ one over y नहीं। y, x का function है, तो chain rule वो extra dy dx माँगता है।
Trap two, u to the v पर half-rule। सिर्फ exponential piece लिखना, या सिर्फ power piece। दोनों सच के आधे हैं; असली answer उनका sum है। u to the v का one-piece answer हमेशा incomplete है।
Trap three, parametric second-derivative ratio। दो second t-derivatives का ratio कभी मत use करो। हमेशा: slope निकालो, t के respect में differentiate करो, फिर rate of x से एक बार और divide करो।
Trap four, positive-base condition ignore करना। log differentiation को positive base चाहिए; अगर base zero या negative हो सकता है, absolute values के साथ काम करो या domain restrict करो, और वो बताओ।
पहला pro-tip: किसी भी u to the v के लिए, फिर से derive मत करो, answer सीधे exponential piece plus power piece लिखो। वो एक line हर variable-power question cover करती है।

दूसरा pro-tip: parametric curves के लिए, कोई value डालने से पहले dy dx पूरी तरह simplify करो। constants लगभग हमेशा cancel होते हैं, और एक clean symbolic slope में substitute करना कहीं कम error-prone है।

board_events.text: The derivative of the derivative
For a moving car: first derivative = speed; second derivative = acceleration.

board_events.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 400 220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M 40 70 Q 110 210 180 70" fill="none" stroke="#1a73e8" stroke-width="3"/><text x="110" y="52" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">concave up (cup)</text><text x="110" y="196" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">holds water</text><path d="M 220 150 Q 290 10 360 150" fill="none" stroke="#d93025" stroke-width="3"/><text x="290" y="178" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">concave down (cap)</text><text x="290" y="28" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">sheds water</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Concavity: y'' positive bends toward the sky (cup); y'' negative bends toward the ground (cap)

board_events.text: First derivative: uphill or downhill. Second derivative: curving toward the sky or the ground.
Parametric and implicit second derivatives follow the earlier rules — no naive ratio, chain each $y$-term.
A sign change of $y''$ marks an inflection point — where concavity flips.

segments.text: <curious>The first derivative measures a rate of change. So what does the derivative of the derivative measure? Something you feel every time you accelerate.

For a moving car, the first derivative is the speedometer reading — how fast position changes. The second derivative measures how fast the rate itself is changing — that is the acceleration, how hard you press the pedal.
In symbols, the second derivative is the derivative of dy dx, written d two y by d x squared, or simply y double dash. You differentiate once, then differentiate the result again.

Geometrically, the second derivative tells you which way a curve bends. Where it is positive, the graph is concave up, a cup that could hold water. Where it is negative, it is concave down, a dome that sheds water.

So the first derivative tells you whether you are going uphill or downhill. The second tells you whether the road is curving toward the sky or toward the ground. They answer completely different questions.

For parametric curves, use the rule from the last subtopic — differentiate the slope by t, divide by the rate of x, never the naive ratio. For implicit relations, differentiate twice, chain-ruling every y term.
And one more reading: where the second derivative changes sign, the concavity flips — that point is an inflection point. The cube root example from the foundations flips exactly at the origin.
<curious>first derivative एक rate of change नापता है। तो derivative का derivative क्या नापता है? कुछ जो आप हर बार accelerate करते समय महसूस करते हो।

एक चलती car के लिए, first derivative speedometer reading है — position कितनी तेज़ी से बदलती है। second derivative नापता है कि rate ख़ुद कितनी तेज़ी से बदल रही है — यही acceleration है, आप pedal कितना ज़ोर से दबाते हो।
Symbols में, second derivative है dy dx का derivative, लिखा जाता है d two y by d x squared, या बस y double dash। आप एक बार differentiate करते हो, फिर result को फिर differentiate करते हो।
Geometrically, second derivative बताता है curve किस तरफ मुड़ता है। जहाँ यह positive है, graph concave up है, एक cup जो पानी रोक सके। जहाँ negative है, concave down है, एक dome जो पानी बहा दे।
तो first derivative बताता है आप uphill जा रहे हो या downhill। second बताता है road आसमान की तरफ मुड़ रहा है या ज़मीन की तरफ। ये बिल्कुल अलग सवालों के जवाब देते हैं।

parametric curves के लिए, पिछले subtopic का rule use करो — slope को t से differentiate, rate of x से divide, कभी naive ratio नहीं। implicit relations के लिए, दो बार differentiate करो, हर y term पर chain rule लगाकर।
और एक reading: जहाँ second derivative sign बदलता है, concavity flip होती है — वो point inflection point है। foundations वाला cube root example exactly origin पर flip करता है।

sections.title: Rolle and the Mean Value Theorem

board_events.text: Two theorems you experience all the time
Rolle: throw a ball up and catch it at the same height — at the top, its velocity is zero.
MVT: drive $150$ km in $2$ hours — at some instant your speedometer read exactly $75$ km/h.

board_events.caption: MVT: some interior tangent (at c) runs parallel to the secant joining a and b

board_events.text: Hypotheses: continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$ (Rolle adds $f(a)=f(b)$). Drop one and the guarantee collapses.

segments.text: Now two Mean Value Theorems that sound abstract but describe something you live through constantly — a ball at its peak, and a speed camera on the expressway.
Start with Rolle. Throw a ball straight up and catch it at the same height it left your hand. At the very top of its flight, for one instant, it is neither rising nor falling — its velocity is zero.

Rolle makes this rigorous: if a smooth, unbroken function has equal values at two points, then somewhere strictly between them the slope must be zero. You went up and came back, so there had to be a flat moment at the turn.

Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem is the grown-up generalization. Drive one hundred fifty kilometres in two hours; your average speed was seventy-five. MVT guarantees that at some instant your speedometer read exactly seventy-five.

In symbols, there is a point c where the instantaneous slope equals the average slope across the interval. Geometrically, some tangent is parallel to the secant joining the endpoints. This is exactly how average-speed cameras catch you.

The picture says it all: the green secant joins the endpoints, and somewhere inside, the dashed tangent at c runs exactly parallel to it. Rolle is just the special case where that secant happens to be horizontal.

Both theorems demand continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval, with Rolle adding equal endpoints. Drop even one and the guarantee collapses — the V on minus one to one has equal heights yet no flat spot, because it is not differentiable at its corner.
अब दो Mean Value Theorems जो abstract लगते हैं पर कुछ ऐसा बताते हैं जो आप लगातार जीते हो — अपने peak पर एक ball, और expressway पर एक speed camera।
Rolle से शुरू। एक ball सीधे ऊपर फेंको और उसी height पर catch करो जहाँ से छोड़ी। उड़ान के बिल्कुल top पर, एक instant के लिए, वो न चढ़ रही है न गिर रही — उसकी velocity zero है।

Rolle इसे rigorous बनाता है: अगर एक smooth, unbroken function के दो points पर equal values हों, तो उनके बीच कहीं strictly slope zero होनी ही चाहिए। आप ऊपर गए और लौटे, तो मोड़ पर एक flat moment होना ही था।

Lagrange का Mean Value Theorem बड़ा generalization है। एक सौ पचास kilometre दो घंटे में चलाओ; आपकी average speed पचहत्तर थी। MVT guarantee करता है कि किसी instant पर आपका speedometer exactly पचहत्तर पढ़ रहा था।

Symbols में, एक point c है जहाँ instantaneous slope, interval की average slope के बराबर है। Geometrically, कोई tangent, endpoints को जोड़ने वाले secant के parallel है। average-speed cameras आपको ठीक इसी तरह पकड़ते हैं।
तस्वीर सब कह देती है: हरा secant endpoints को जोड़ता है, और अंदर कहीं, c पर dashed tangent उसके exactly parallel चलता है। Rolle बस वो special case है जहाँ वो secant horizontal होता है।

दोनों theorems closed interval पर continuity और open interval पर differentiability माँगते हैं, Rolle equal endpoints जोड़ता है। एक भी छोड़ो और guarantee collapse — minus one to one पर V की equal heights हैं फिर भी कोई flat spot नहीं, क्योंकि वो अपने corner पर differentiable नहीं।

sections.subtopic: Second-Order Derivatives & the Mean Value Theorems
sections.title: Definitions and the validity conditions

board_events.text: The precise statements to quote in exams

board_events.latex: \text{Parametric: } y'' = \frac{\frac{d}{dt}(dy/dx)}{dx/dt}; \quad \text{Implicit: differentiate twice, each } y \text{ carries } \tfrac{dy}{dx}
\text{Rolle: } f \text{ cont. on } [a,b],\; \text{diff. on } (a,b),\; f(a)=f(b) \Rightarrow \exists\, c: f'(c)=0
\text{Lagrange: } f \text{ cont. on } [a,b],\; \text{diff. on } (a,b) \Rightarrow \exists\, c: f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}

board_events.text: Both are existence theorems: they guarantee at least one $c$, say nothing about uniqueness, and you still solve for it.
Validity: confirm continuity on $[a,b]$ and differentiability on $(a,b)$ first — any corner, cusp, or break inside voids the theorem.

segments.text: Let's pin down the exact statements you quote in an answer: the second-derivative forms, then Rolle and Lagrange with their hypotheses spelled out.
The second derivative is the derivative of the first derivative, and its sign gives concavity: positive is a cup, negative is a cap. That is the direct case for an explicit function of x.

Two carried-over forms: for parametric, differentiate the slope by t and divide by the rate of x, never the naive ratio. For implicit, differentiate the relation twice, remembering each y term carries a dy dx factor.

Rolle's theorem: if f is continuous on the closed interval, differentiable on the open interval, and takes equal values at the endpoints, then there exists at least one c inside where the derivative is zero.

Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem: with the same continuity and differentiability, but no equal-endpoints requirement, there exists at least one c inside where the instantaneous slope equals the average slope.
Read the fine print: both are existence theorems. They guarantee at least one such c exists, but say nothing about whether it is unique, and you still have to solve for it yourself.

The validity conditions are the hypotheses themselves: always confirm continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval, plus equal endpoints for Rolle, before using either conclusion. Any corner, cusp, or break inside voids the theorem.
चलिए वो exact statements pin करते हैं जो आप answer में quote करते हो: second-derivative forms, फिर Rolle और Lagrange अपनी hypotheses के साथ।
second derivative, first derivative का derivative है, और इसका sign concavity देता है: positive एक cup, negative एक cap। यह x के explicit function के लिए direct case है।

दो carried-over forms: parametric के लिए, slope को t से differentiate करो और rate of x से divide करो, कभी naive ratio नहीं। implicit के लिए, relation को दो बार differentiate करो, याद रखते हुए हर y term एक dy dx factor रखता है।
Rolle's theorem: अगर f, closed interval पर continuous, open interval पर differentiable, और endpoints पर equal values ले, तो अंदर कम से कम एक c है जहाँ derivative zero है।
Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem: वही continuity और differentiability के साथ, पर equal-endpoints की शर्त बिना, अंदर कम से कम एक c है जहाँ instantaneous slope, average slope के बराबर है।
Fine print पढ़ो: दोनों existence theorems हैं। ये guarantee करते हैं कम से कम एक ऐसा c है, पर यह नहीं कहते कि वो unique है, और आपको उसे ख़ुद solve करना है।

Validity conditions ख़ुद hypotheses हैं: किसी भी conclusion use करने से पहले, हमेशा closed interval पर continuity और open interval पर differentiability confirm करो, plus Rolle के लिए equal endpoints। अंदर कोई भी corner, cusp, या break theorem को void कर देता है।

sections.title: MVT from Rolle, and a y''-2y'+2y=0 relation

board_events.text: The auxiliary-function proof, plus a second-order relation

board_events.latex: y = e^{x}\sin x \;\Rightarrow\; y' = e^{x}(\sin x + \cos x)

segments.text: First the cleanest proof in the subtopic — deriving MVT from Rolle — then a Board-favourite second-order relation to prove.

Rolle only fires when the endpoints are level, so we tilt the function to make them level. Define an auxiliary g of x as f minus the straight secant line joining the two endpoints. So g measures the vertical gap between the curve and the secant.

At the endpoints the curve meets the secant, so the gap is zero at both. g is continuous and differentiable because it is f minus a polynomial. We have manufactured exactly the equal-endpoints condition Rolle needs.
Apply Rolle to g: there exists a c inside the interval where g dash of c is zero. That single application is the whole engine of the proof.

Differentiate g: g dash is f dash minus the constant average slope. Setting g dash of c to zero gives f dash of c equals the average slope. That is Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem, proved. Subtracting the secant was the whole trick.
Now the relation. For y equals e to the x sine x, the product rule gives y dash equals e to the x sine x plus e to the x cosine x, which factors as e to the x times sine x plus cosine x.

Differentiate again: y double dash comes out as two e to the x cosine x. Substitute into y double dash minus two y dash plus two y, and every term cancels in pairs, leaving zero. The relation holds. Proof complete.
पहले subtopic का सबसे clean proof — Rolle से MVT निकालना — फिर एक Board-favourite second-order relation prove करने के लिए।

Rolle सिर्फ तब चलता है जब endpoints level हों, तो हम function को tilt करके उन्हें level बनाते हैं। एक auxiliary g of x define करो, f minus वो straight secant line जो दोनों endpoints को जोड़ती है। तो g, curve और secant के बीच vertical gap नापता है।

endpoints पर curve, secant से मिलती है, तो gap दोनों पर zero है। g continuous और differentiable है क्योंकि यह f minus एक polynomial है। हमने exactly वो equal-endpoints condition बना ली जो Rolle को चाहिए।
g पर Rolle लगाओ: interval के अंदर एक c है जहाँ g dash of c zero है। वो एक application ही proof का पूरा engine है।

g differentiate करो: g dash है f dash minus constant average slope। g dash of c को zero करने पर f dash of c equals average slope मिलता है। यही Lagrange का Mean Value Theorem है, proved। secant घटाना ही पूरा trick था।
अब relation। y equals e to the x sine x के लिए, product rule देता है y dash equals e to the x sine x plus e to the x cosine x, जो e to the x times sine x plus cosine x में factor होता है।

फिर differentiate करो: y double dash निकलता है two e to the x cosine x। y double dash minus two y dash plus two y में substitute करो, और हर term जोड़ों में cancel होता है, बचता है zero। relation holds। Proof complete।

sections.title: Verifying Rolle, and the |x-1| hypothesis trap

board_events.text: A clean verification and a hidden hypothesis failure
The derivative is $-1$ on the left, $+1$ on the right — never zero. Panic?
The resolution: differentiability fails at the corner $x = 1 \in (0,2)$, so Rolle does not apply — the conclusion is not promised.

segments.text: Two examples: verifying Rolle cleanly for sine, then the classic trap where the obvious condition holds but a hidden hypothesis quietly fails.
Verify Rolle for sine x on the interval zero to pi, and find the point c. First we check all three hypotheses hold.
Sine is continuous and differentiable everywhere, so certainly on this interval. The endpoints: sine of zero is zero, and sine of pi is also zero, so the values are equal. All three conditions hold.

Now find c: set f dash of c, which is cosine c, equal to zero. That gives c equals pi over two, which lies strictly inside the interval. Rolle is verified — the tangent at the peak of the sine curve is horizontal.

<curious>Now the trap. Apply Rolle to the absolute value of x minus one on zero to two. The endpoints look perfect: f of zero is one, f of two is one, so the equal-endpoints condition holds. A student charges ahead…
…tries to solve f dash of c equals zero, finds the derivative is minus one on the left and plus one on the right, never zero, and panics, assuming an arithmetic error. But there is no error.

The resolution: Rolle simply does not apply. The differentiability hypothesis fails at the corner x equals one, inside the interval. With a hypothesis violated, the conclusion is not promised — and indeed it fails. Always validate continuity and differentiability before reaching for the conclusion.
दो examples: sine के लिए Rolle को cleanly verify करना, फिर वो classic trap जहाँ obvious condition पूरी होती है पर एक hidden hypothesis चुपचाप fail हो जाती है।
sine x के लिए Rolle को interval zero to pi पर verify करो, और point c निकालो। पहले हम check करते हैं तीनों hypotheses पूरी होती हैं।
sine हर जगह continuous और differentiable है, तो इस interval पर ज़रूर। endpoints: sine of zero, zero है, और sine of pi भी zero है, तो values equal हैं। तीनों conditions पूरी।
अब c निकालो: f dash of c, यानी cosine c, को zero करो। वो देता है c equals pi over two, जो interval के अंदर strictly है। Rolle verified — sine curve के peak पर tangent horizontal है।

<curious>अब trap। absolute value of x minus one पर zero to two पर Rolle लगाओ। endpoints perfect दिखते हैं: f of zero, one है, f of two, one है, तो equal-endpoints condition पूरी। एक student आगे बढ़ जाता है…
…f dash of c equals zero solve करने की कोशिश करता है, पाता है derivative left पर minus one और right पर plus one है, कभी zero नहीं, और घबरा जाता है, arithmetic error मानकर। पर कोई error नहीं है।

Resolution: Rolle apply ही नहीं होता। differentiability hypothesis, corner x equals one पर fail होती है, interval के अंदर। एक hypothesis violate होने पर, conclusion promised नहीं — और सच में fail होती है। conclusion तक पहुँचने से पहले हमेशा continuity और differentiability validate करो।

sections.title: MVT as a tool: proving an inequality

board_events.text: An apparently unprovable inequality falls in three lines

segments.text: <excited>The signature power of MVT: choose the right function, and an apparently unprovable inequality falls out in just three lines.
The target: for zero less than a less than b, show that b minus a over b is less than log of b over a, which is less than b minus a over a. Two inequalities to pin at once.
The move is to apply the Mean Value Theorem to f of x equals log x on the interval a to b. Log x is continuous and differentiable for positive x, so the hypotheses hold.
MVT gives a c between a and b where f dash of c equals the average slope. Since the derivative of log is one over x, this reads one over c equals log of b over a, over b minus a.

Now the key step. Because c lies strictly between a and b, all positive, reciprocating reverses the order: one over b is less than one over c, which is less than one over a. Reciprocals flip inequalities for positive numbers.
Substitute one over c as log of b over a, over b minus a, into the middle. Now the sandwich reads one over b, less than log of b over a over b minus a, less than one over a.

Finish by multiplying throughout by b minus a, which is positive, so the inequalities are preserved. Out drops exactly the target: b minus a over b, less than log b over a, less than b minus a over a. Choose the right function and the bounds on c read straight off.
<excited>MVT की signature ताक़त: सही function चुनो, और एक apparently unprovable inequality सिर्फ तीन lines में गिर जाती है।
Target: zero less than a less than b के लिए, दिखाओ कि b minus a over b, log of b over a से कम है, जो b minus a over a से कम है। एक साथ दो inequalities pin करनी हैं।
चाल है Mean Value Theorem को f of x equals log x पर interval a to b पर लगाना। log x, positive x के लिए continuous और differentiable है, तो hypotheses पूरी।
MVT एक c देता है a और b के बीच जहाँ f dash of c, average slope के बराबर है। चूँकि log का derivative one over x है, यह पढ़ता है one over c equals log of b over a, over b minus a।

अब key step। चूँकि c, a और b के बीच strictly है, सब positive, reciprocate करना order उलट देता है: one over b, one over c से कम है, जो one over a से कम है। reciprocals positive numbers के लिए inequalities flip करते हैं।
one over c को log of b over a, over b minus a, बीच में substitute करो। अब sandwich पढ़ता है one over b, less than log of b over a over b minus a, less than one over a।

b minus a से पूरे multiply करके ख़त्म करो, जो positive है, तो inequalities preserve होती हैं। निकलता है exactly target: b minus a over b, less than log b over a, less than b minus a over a। सही function चुनो और c पर bounds सीधे पढ़ लो।

board_events.text: Four traps, and two default weapons
Trap 1: applying a theorem without checking hypotheses — the $|x|$ / step-function / piecewise trap.
Trap 2: confusing Rolle with MVT — Rolle needs $f(a)=f(b)$ and concludes $f'(c)=0$.
Trap 3: accepting a $c$ outside the open interval — it must lie strictly inside $(a,b)$.
Trap 4: the parametric/implicit second-derivative slip again — never the naive ratio.

board_events.latex: \text{For inequalities: pick } f \text{ so } f'(c) \text{ is the quantity to bound, then squeeze with } a\lt c\lt b

board_events.text: For “how many roots,” reach for Rolle: two roots always manufacture a zero of $f'$ between them. Rolle = MVT with a horizontal secant.

segments.text: Let's bank the second-order and Mean-Value mistakes, and the two default strategies for the hardest questions.

Trap one, applying a theorem without checking hypotheses. The classic absolute-value, greatest-integer, or piecewise trap satisfies the obvious condition while quietly breaking continuity or differentiability. Always validate both first.

Trap two, confusing Rolle with MVT. Rolle additionally needs equal endpoints and concludes the slope is zero; MVT needs no such equality and concludes the slope equals the average. Using slope equals zero when the endpoints differ is wrong.
Trap three, accepting a c outside the open interval. The guaranteed point must lie strictly inside a to b. A solution landing on an endpoint does not count toward verifying the theorem.

Trap four, the same second-derivative slip from the parametric subtopic. Never write y double dash as the ratio of the two second t-derivatives. Differentiate the slope by t, then divide by the rate of x again.

The first pro-tip, for JEE Advanced: MVT is the default weapon for inequality proofs. Choose f so that f dash of c is exactly the quantity you want to bound, then squeeze using a less than c less than b.

The second pro-tip: for how-many-roots questions, reach for Rolle — two roots always manufacture a zero of the derivative between them. And remember, Rolle is just MVT with a horizontal secant: learn one picture, get both.
चलिए second-order और Mean-Value mistakes bank करते हैं, और सबसे hard questions के लिए दो default strategies।

Trap one, hypotheses check किए बिना theorem apply करना। classic absolute-value, greatest-integer, या piecewise trap obvious condition पूरी करता है पर चुपचाप continuity या differentiability तोड़ता है। हमेशा पहले दोनों validate करो।

Trap two, Rolle को MVT से confuse करना। Rolle को अतिरिक्त equal endpoints चाहिए और slope zero निकालता है; MVT को ऐसी कोई equality नहीं चाहिए और slope equals average निकालता है। endpoints अलग होने पर slope equals zero use करना ग़लत है।
Trap three, open interval के बाहर एक c स्वीकारना। guaranteed point, a to b के अंदर strictly होना चाहिए। endpoint पर आने वाला solution theorem verify करने में नहीं गिना जाता।
Trap four, parametric subtopic वाला वही second-derivative slip। y double dash को कभी दो second t-derivatives का ratio मत लिखो। slope को t से differentiate करो, फिर rate of x से फिर divide करो।
पहला pro-tip, JEE Advanced के लिए: inequality proofs के लिए MVT default weapon है। f ऐसा चुनो कि f dash of c exactly वो quantity हो जिसे bound करना है, फिर a less than c less than b से squeeze करो।

दूसरा pro-tip: how-many-roots questions के लिए, Rolle की तरफ जाओ — दो roots हमेशा उनके बीच derivative का एक zero बना देती हैं। और याद रखो, Rolle बस horizontal secant वाला MVT है: एक तस्वीर सीखो, दोनों पाओ।

board_events.text: Everything pointwise: check continuity before differentiability; state domains and principal ranges; both MVTs are existence results.

segments.text: Here is your complete toolkit for the chapter, gathered onto one board. This is a recap, not a re-teach — read each line as a trigger for what you already understand.

Continuity at a point: left-hand limit equals right-hand limit equals the value. Differentiability: the two one-sided derivatives are equal and finite. And the bridge — differentiable implies continuous, one way only.
The toolkit basics: the power rule, the trig derivatives, the product rule with its two terms, and the quotient rule — low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared.
The chain rule: rates multiply along the chain. Its patterns — sine of g, e to the g, log of g — each carry the inner derivative g dash as a factor. Never forget that factor.
Implicit differentiation: every y term carries a dy dx, and mixed x-y terms use the product rule. Then gather the dy dx terms and solve; the answer involves both x and y.

Inverse trig: inverse sine gives one over root one minus x squared, inverse tan gives one over one plus x squared, cofunctions carry a minus. And the golden identity, two inverse tan of x equals inverse tan of two x over one minus x squared — mind the range.

Logarithmic and parametric: u to the v is the exponential piece plus the power piece. Parametric slope is the ratio of the t-rates; the parametric second derivative is slope differentiated by t, over the rate of x — never the naive ratio.
And the Mean Value Theorems: Rolle, with equal endpoints, guarantees a zero slope inside. Lagrange guarantees an interior slope equal to the average slope. Rolle is just MVT with a horizontal secant.

One closing reminder that ties the whole chapter together: everything here is pointwise. Check continuity before differentiability, state your domains and principal ranges, and treat both Mean Value Theorems as existence results — they promise a c, and you still solve for it.
यहाँ chapter का आपका complete toolkit है, एक ही board पर इकट्ठा। यह recap है, दोबारा पढ़ाना नहीं — हर line को उस चीज़ के trigger की तरह पढ़ो जो आप पहले से समझते हो।
एक point पर continuity: left-hand limit equals right-hand limit equals value। Differentiability: दो one-sided derivatives equal और finite। और bridge — differentiable implies continuous, सिर्फ एक तरफ।
Toolkit basics: power rule, trig derivatives, product rule अपने दो terms के साथ, और quotient rule — low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared।
Chain rule: rates chain के साथ multiply होती हैं। इसके patterns — sine of g, e to the g, log of g — हर एक inner derivative g dash को factor की तरह रखता है। वो factor कभी मत भूलो।
Implicit differentiation: हर y term एक dy dx रखता है, और mixed x-y terms product rule use करते हैं। फिर dy dx terms इकट्ठा करके solve करो; answer x और y दोनों रखता है।

Inverse trig: inverse sine देता है one over root one minus x squared, inverse tan देता है one over one plus x squared, cofunctions minus रखते हैं। और golden identity, two inverse tan of x equals inverse tan of two x over one minus x squared — range का ध्यान।

Logarithmic और parametric: u to the v है exponential piece plus power piece। parametric slope, t-rates का ratio है; parametric second derivative है slope को t से differentiate, over rate of x — कभी naive ratio नहीं।

और Mean Value Theorems: Rolle, equal endpoints के साथ, अंदर एक zero slope guarantee करता है। Lagrange एक interior slope guarantee करता है जो average slope के बराबर है। Rolle बस horizontal secant वाला MVT है।

एक closing reminder जो पूरे chapter को जोड़ता है: यहाँ सब कुछ pointwise है। continuity, differentiability से पहले check करो, अपने domains और principal ranges बताओ, और दोनों Mean Value Theorems को existence results मानो — वे एक c का वादा करते हैं, और उसे आप ख़ुद solve करते हो।

board_events.text: Last-minute recall before the exam
DiCo, not CoDi: Differentiable $\Rightarrow$ Continuous, but Continuous does not $\Rightarrow$ Differentiable.
Piecewise: test only junction points; always continuity first, differentiability second.
Product = two strips; Quotient = low d-high minus high d-low, over low-squared.
Chain rule: outside-in, and don't forget the inside — one factor per layer.
Implicit: every $y$ owes a $\frac{dy}{dx}$ — it's just the chain rule in disguise.
Inverse trig: $\tfrac{2x}{1-x^{2}} \to \tan\theta$, $2x\sqrt{1-x^{2}} \to \sin\theta$, $\sqrt{x^{2}-1} \to \sec\theta$ — mind the range.
Parametric $y''$: slope, differentiate by $t$, divide by $dx/dt$ — NOT $\frac{d^{2}y/dt^{2}}{d^{2}x/dt^{2}}$. Log diff: never drop the $\frac{1}{y}$.
Rolle = MVT with a horizontal secant; check hypotheses first; both give at least one interior $c$.

segments.text: A fast-recall sweep of the whole chapter — the one-liners and mnemonics to flash through the night before the exam.
Foundations: DiCo, not CoDi — differentiable implies continuous, but continuous does not imply differentiable. Smoothness fails at corners, cusps, and every discontinuity.
Strategy: for piecewise functions test only the junction points, never the smooth interiors, and always run continuity first, differentiability second. The first failure settles the question.
Toolkit: a product's derivative is always two strips, and the quotient rhyme is low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared. A one-term answer to a product is wrong by inspection.
Chain rule: outside-in, and do not forget the inside. Every peeled layer owes a factor, so count your factors against your layers as a completeness check.
Implicit: it is just the chain rule in disguise — every y owes a dy dx, and mixed terms use the product rule. A y-term with no dy dx means you dropped a chain factor.

Inverse trig: substitute, collapse the double angle, then differentiate, and mind the range. Two x over one minus x squared points to tan theta; two x root one minus x squared to sine theta; root x squared minus one to secant theta.

Log and parametric: for u to the v write exponential piece plus power piece, and never drop the one over y. For the parametric second derivative — slope, differentiate by t, divide by the rate of x — never the naive ratio.

And the Mean Value Theorems: Rolle is MVT with a horizontal secant. Check the hypotheses first, accept only a c strictly inside the interval, and remember both are existence results. That is the whole chapter in one breath — go get the marks.
पूरे chapter का fast-recall sweep — वो one-liners और mnemonics जो exam से एक रात पहले flash करने हैं।
Foundations: DiCo, not CoDi — differentiable implies continuous, पर continuous, differentiable imply नहीं करता। smoothness corners, cusps, और हर discontinuity पर fail होती है।
Strategy: piecewise functions में सिर्फ junction points test करो, कभी smooth interiors नहीं, और हमेशा continuity पहले, differentiability बाद में। पहला failure सवाल settle कर देता है।
Toolkit: product का derivative हमेशा two strips है, और quotient rhyme है low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared। product का one-term answer देखते ही ग़लत है।
Chain rule: outside-in, and don't forget the inside। हर peeled layer एक factor का क़र्ज़दार है, तो factors को layers के ख़िलाफ़ गिनो, completeness check की तरह।
Implicit: यह बस chain rule का भेस है — हर y एक dy dx का क़र्ज़दार है, और mixed terms product rule use करते हैं। बिना dy dx वाला y-term मतलब आपने एक chain factor drop किया।

Inverse trig: substitute, double angle collapse करो, फिर differentiate, और range का ध्यान। two x over one minus x squared, tan theta की तरफ; two x root one minus x squared, sine theta; root x squared minus one, secant theta।

Log और parametric: u to the v के लिए exponential piece plus power piece लिखो, और one over y कभी drop मत करो। parametric second derivative के लिए — slope, t से differentiate, rate of x से divide — कभी naive ratio नहीं।

और Mean Value Theorems: Rolle, horizontal secant वाला MVT है। पहले hypotheses check करो, सिर्फ interval के अंदर strictly एक c स्वीकारो, और याद रखो दोनों existence results हैं। यही पूरा chapter एक साँस में — जाओ marks लो।
